title: Curate one sample’s annotations and write results back to the DB
text:
Reads the reconciled annotations, the sample's curate_opts ruleset, any
per-feature reference identities (blast_ref_alignment), and the sample vs.
hit lineages, runs curate_rrna_core(), then updates each feature's
status/flags and the per-sample annotate summary (n_flags,
curate_flags) in one transaction. partial_start/partial_stop are only
set (to 1) where still NULL, so a curator's own choice is kept.

title: Initialize a new RiboPilot project
text:
Mirrors MitoPilot's new_project(). Creates the project directory, copies
the mapping file, initializes the SQLite tracking database, and writes a
.config Nextflow config from the chosen executor template.

title: Initialize a new RiboPilot project
text:
Usage
new_project(
  path = ".",
  mapping_fn = NULL,
  mapping_id = "ID",
  data_path = NULL,
  assembly_path = NULL,
  min_depth = 2e+06,
  executor = c("docker", "conda", "local", "slurm", "pbs", "sge", "lsf", "NMNH_Hydra",
    "NOAA_SEDNA"),
  container = paste0("macguigand/ribopilot:", utils::packageVersion("RiboPilot")),
  custom_seeds_db = NULL,
  custom_labels_db = NULL,
  ref_dir = NULL,
  config = NULL,
  profile_dir = ribopilot_config_dir(),
  ncbi_api_key = NULL,
  check_reads = TRUE,
  check_assemblies = TRUE,
  mapping_geome = "GEOME_BCID",
  fetch_geome = TRUE,
  mapping_gbif = "GBIF_ID",
  fetch_gbif = TRUE,
  mapping_ncbi = "BioSample",
  fetch_ncbi = TRUE,
  link_sources = FALSE,
  Rproj = TRUE,
  force = FALSE,
  ...
)

title: Initialize a new RiboPilot project
text:
Arguments

path

Path to the project directory (default = current working dir).


mapping_fn

Path to a comma-separated mapping file. Minimally an ID
column (unique sample id), a Taxon column, and R1/R2 columns naming
the paired read files relative to data_path (or an Assembly column).
Column names are matched ignoring case. Extra metadata columns are
preserved.


mapping_id

Column in the mapping file with unique ids (default "ID").


data_path

Directory where the raw read data is located. Required
when any sample lists reads; not needed when every sample supplies its own
assembly.


assembly_path

Directory holding the assembly files named in the
mapping file's optional Assembly column. A sample with an assembly is
searched for its nuclear rDNA contigs instead of being assembled from
reads, and its R1/R2 may be left blank. See
dev/design/20_USER_ASSEMBLIES.md.


min_depth

Minimum number of reads left after trimming, counting both
reads of a pair (2000000 is 1000000 pairs). A sample below it is not
assembled and is marked Failed with a note.


executor

Executor for the Nextflow pipeline. Ready to use as-is:
"docker" (default) and "local" run the RiboPilot container on this
machine, and "NMNH_Hydra" and "NOAA_SEDNA" are ready-made Singularity
profiles for those clusters. "conda" uses a self-installed conda env (not
supported; warns). For any other cluster, build a profile with
generate_config() and pass its name here. A bare scheduler name ("slurm",
"sge", "pbs", "lsf") is an error: it has no queue or cluster options yet.


container

Container to use for pipeline execution.


custom_seeds_db

Path/URL to a custom GetOrganelle nr seeds database.


custom_labels_db

Path/URL to a custom GetOrganelle nr labels database.


ref_dir

Folder for built reference databases (default: the
RIBOPILOT_REF_DIR environment variable, else ribopilot_ref_dir()).


config

Optional path to an existing custom Nextflow config file.


profile_dir

Directory searched for saved cluster profiles.


ncbi_api_key

Optional NCBI API key (raises request rate limits).


check_reads

(logical) Check that the read files named in the mapping
file exist under data_path (default TRUE). Set FALSE when the data will
be staged later.


check_assemblies

(logical) Check that the assembly files named in the
mapping file exist under assembly_path (default TRUE).


mapping_geome

Name of the mapping-file column holding GEOME BCIDs
(optional). Stored as GEOME_BCID. See vignette("Sample-Metadata").
Passed to new_db().


fetch_geome

Fetch GEOME metadata for samples with a BCID during setup
(default TRUE). Set FALSE when offline and run fetch_geome() later.
Passed to new_db().


mapping_gbif

Name of the mapping-file column holding GBIF occurrence
IDs (optional). Stored as GBIF_ID. See vignette("Sample-Metadata").
Passed to new_db().


fetch_gbif

Fetch GBIF metadata for samples with a GBIF ID during setup
(default TRUE). Set FALSE when offline and run fetch_gbif() later.
Passed to new_db().


mapping_ncbi

Name of the mapping-file column holding NCBI
BioSample or SRA accessions (optional). Must not be the sample ID column.
Stored as BioSample. See vignette("Sample-Metadata").
Passed to new_db().


fetch_ncbi

Fetch NCBI metadata for samples with a BioSample
value during setup (default TRUE). Set FALSE when offline and run
fetch_ncbi() later.
Passed to new_db().


link_sources

Follow links between GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI records to
fill in IDs a sample does not have yet (default FALSE). Saved as the project
setting. See vignette("Sample-Metadata").
Passed to new_db().


Rproj

(logical) Initialize/open an RStudio project (default TRUE; no
effect outside RStudio).


force

(logical) Recreate an existing project database (default
FALSE). Without it, new_project() stops when the folder already holds a
project.


...

Additional default processing parameters passed to new_db().

Fetch GEOME metadata for samples with a BCID
when the samples are added

fetch_gbif

Fetch GBIF metadata for samples with a GBIF ID

mapping_ncbi

title: What would bulk triage do, without doing it
text:
A bulk write across a whole project is the highest-blast-radius action in the
app, so it is never applied without showing the count first – including how
many samples would end up with NOTHING kept, which is the outcome that
silently loses a sample.

title: What would bulk triage do, without doing it
text:
Usage
triage_preview(con, ids, opts = NULL, overwrite_user = FALSE)

title: What would bulk triage do, without doing it
text:
Arguments

con

Open project DB connection.


ids

Sample IDs to consider.


opts

Named list of per-rule actions; NULL reads the sample's
triage_opts preset.


overwrite_user

Include units a curator decided by hand.

title: What would bulk triage do, without doing it
text:
Value
list with, for the END STATE after Apply: n_units, n_drop, n_undecided,
n_keep, n_samples, emptied, n_user_skipped, n_locked_skipped, by_rule; and,
for what Apply would actually CHANGE: n_changed (units that are not skipped
and whose stored triage/reason/rule differ from the proposed ones, by the
same comparison auto_triage_sample() uses to decide what to write), broken
down by proposed verdict into n_new_drop, n_new_keep and n_new_flag, which
therefore sum to n_changed.

title: What would bulk triage do, without doing it
text:
Details
If every rule is "off" for a sample, that sample is treated as fully skipped:
the preview reports its CURRENT stored state unchanged, with zero counted in
every n_new_* counter and in n_changed. See
dev/design/09_TRIAGE_RULES_AND_DEPTH.md section 3.3.

title: Select nuclear rDNA contigs from a barrnap scan
text:
Given the merged barrnap GFF for one sample's supplied assembly, keep the
contigs that carry a nuclear rDNA anchor. A contig qualifies on an 18S or a
28S hit; a lone 5.8S hit does not, because 5.8S is short enough that a single
hit is as likely to be a degraded pseudogene copy as a real repeat unit.

text:

select_rrna_contigs(gff_lines, lengths = NULL, max_contigs = 10)

title: Select nuclear rDNA contigs from a barrnap scan
text:
Arguments

gff_lines

Character vector, the merged barrnap GFF.


lengths

Optional named numeric of contig lengths, names = contig ids.


max_contigs

Most contigs to keep, best first (default 10). Fed from

scheduler

(Docker on one machine, the same as executor = "local").

Optional raw clusterOptions string appended verbatim.

SGE parallel environment (default "mthread").

Directory to save the profile in.


interactive

If TRUE and interactive, prompt for unset values.

Overwrite an existing profile (default FALSE).

title: News
text:
Opening the app in Safari now shows a warning on every launch that Safari has known display and interaction issues and suggests Chrome or Firefox.





Longer help text across the app moved behind “?” icons and was shortened: options windows, export window, NMNH voucher report, details windows, triage, trim, reference settings, and the cluster job script.
Every “?” icon now looks and behaves the same: click to open, one open at a time, closes on click away or Escape. Tool documentation keeps its wide scrolling panel.
The Chimera check panel says “features” where it said “genes”.





The Partial column is now Completeness and is worked out automatically: a contig is “complete” when all five features are present and no gene end is partial, otherwise “partial”. It can be sorted and filtered. The Mark Partial buttons are gone; set a gene end with the 5’ and 3’ buttons in the contig window instead. The {partial} export token follows the same rule.
The two sliding-window BLAST tracks in the sequence viewer are now labeled “window” (Window BLAST identity, Window BLAST taxon), grouped by a bracket, to tell them apart from Feature BLAST.
The sequence viewer has a Feature BLAST track above the window BLAST tracks: one block per feature, green for OK, orange for a weak or low-confidence match, red for off-target or non-rDNA, grey for no hit or not searched. In the contig window, clicking a block opens the Feature BLAST table.
Hovering the sequence viewer now shows only the value of the track under the pointer, and its help moved behind a “?” icon beside the viewer title.
Contigs that are both locked and excluded have their own red lock icon, sort position, and Lock filter option.





The annotate and curate option links grey out when the sample’s annotation is locked, like the other option links do for a locked assembly.





Assign Group now offers the groups that already exist, and warns when a selected contig is already in another group.
Clear Group asks for confirmation first.
The Export table has an Exported filter (Yes / No).





Tables in the Run reports, Assemble, and other detail windows showed only a sliver of their rows in Safari: the horizontal scrollbar covered the last row and a vertical scrollbar appeared. Tables that size to their rows now include the bar.
A new project’s .config file is readable by your group (mode 0640, was 0600), so others in the group can work with a shared project.





A new check predicts the two BLAST flags GenBank’s rRNA/ITS curation raises before it assigns accessions: top-hit query coverage under 75% (“Query coverage is less than 75%”) and a top hit aligned in more than one piece (“HSP_problem”). RiboPilot runs NCBI’s own searches (default megablast against ITS_eukaryote_sequences and the SSU/LSU eukaryote rRNA sets) on each contig in the annotation step and again on the recheck, and stores the result as genbank_check. It reproduces NCBI’s reply exactly on the ten records of SUB16547976.
The result shows in the Checks column (amber, never a gate), in a GenBank BLAST column on the scaffold and Annotation Review tables, and at export: a genbank_check column in <group>_summary.csv and the HTML report, a count of flagged records in the Export done window, and a README section with NCBI’s wording. See “The GenBank BLAST check” in the GenBank Submission guide.
Most fish records trip both flags because the ITS database holds few fishes; the flags predict GenBank’s reply, not a bad assembly.
The check needs ITS_eukaryote_sequences beside the panel. rDNA panel 2026.08.18.2 ships it and is included in the 0.1.2 container image. With an older panel every contig stores not_run(no ITS_eukaryote_sequences database).
Project database version 7: genbank_check columns on annotate and review_units. Contigs already locked keep not_run(not checked) until they are unlocked and rechecked.





The rDNA BLAST panel is 2026.08.18.2. The rDNA sequences are the same as in 2026.08.18.1; this release adds NCBI’s ITS_eukaryote_sequences database for the GenBank BLAST check and refreshes the NCBI 16S and taxonomy databases shipped beside the panel.





clear_ref_cache() deletes the cached reference data in the shared reference folder (clade databases, record counts, and stored reference sequences). It affects every project that uses the folder, so it lists what it found, asks you to type clear, and refuses to run from a script. The BLAST panel and container images are left alone.

title: Smithsonian Hydra setup
text:
This page covers what is specific to the Smithsonian Hydra cluster. Once you are set up here, continue with the Get started walkthrough, but using executor = "NMNH_Hydra" for the new_test_project() function. Running on a cluster has general instructions for using RiboPilot on a cluster.
If you need a Hydra account, see the Hydra policies page.

title: Smithsonian Hydra setup
section: Get an R session on Hydra
text:
Get an R session on Hydra
The simplest route is the dedicated RStudio Server at https://galaxy.si.edu/R4. Log in from a browser with your Hydra credentials. This is a shared resource, so use it for interactive work and submit larger runs as jobs. Details are on the Hydra RStudio page.

title: Smithsonian Hydra setup
text:
Install Nextflow
Hydra has no Nextflow module, so install your own copy once. Run these commands in a terminal connected to Hydra:
cd ~
module load tools/java/21.0.2
curl -s https://get.nextflow.io | bash
chmod +x nextflow
mkdir -p ~/bin
mv nextflow ~/bin/nextflow
echo 'export PATH="${HOME}/bin:${PATH}"' >> ~/.bashrc
source ~/.bashrc
Job scripts written by the app load Java and read ~/.bashrc for you. If you want to use Nextflow from a shell yourself, run module load tools/java/21.0.2 first.

title: Smithsonian Hydra setup
text:
Install RiboPilot
In the R console of your RStudio Server session, follow step 5 of Install the tools. Singularity is already on Hydra, so there is nothing else to install.

title: Smithsonian Hydra setup
text:
Create a project
RiboPilot::new_test_project(
  path = "/pool/public/genomics/<USER>/RiboPilot/test_project",
  executor = "NMNH_Hydra"
)
Use the same executor = "NMNH_Hydra" with RiboPilot::new_project() for your own data. Work under /pool or /scratch. Home folders are too small, and projects cannot run from /store.
By default Singularity’s download cache and the reference folder also sit in your home folder. Disk space, caches, and offline use shows how to move them.

title: Smithsonian Hydra setup
text:
Open the app and run
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("/pool/public/genomics/<USER>/RiboPilot/test_project")
The Update run window shows a job script that is sent to Hydra’s queue for workflow managers. Press Submit as job, or Save script to submit it yourself with qsub. The job keeps going after you close the browser. Watch it with qstat in a terminal, then press the reload button above the table to see new results. Submit a run as a job has the details.
The Get started walkthrough marks each place where Hydra differs, in boxes tagged HYDRA.

title: Sample metadata: GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI
text:
RiboPilot can optionally link each sample to corresponding NCBI, GBIF, or GEOME records. This information can be shown in the app, flagged where databases disagree, and used in your FASTA headers for submission to GenBank.
RiboPilot never merges values or picks one source over another. Each source keeps its own fields, and you decide which ones go into your FASTA headers. Records are not live: if the remote database changes, fetch again. Fetched data never changes how RiboPilot resolves taxonomy.
Related pages:

title: Sample metadata: GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI
text:
Finding the identifiers

GEOME BCID. Open a record on geome-db.org and copy its identifier, which starts with ark:/. Use the most specific record that matches your sequenced material, usually the tissue: RiboPilot also fetches the sample, collecting event, expedition, and project above it.
gbifID. Open the occurrence on gbif.org and copy the number at the end of its address (https://www.gbif.org/occurrence/6186461308).
Smithsonian EZID. NMNH specimens can use their EZID, a permanent identifier starting with ark:/65665/, in place of a gbifID. RiboPilot finds the matching GBIF occurrence, so the specimen must be on GBIF. EZIDs are more stable than gbifIDs. Links from n2t.net or collections.nmnh.si.edu work, with or without dashes.
BioSample or SRA accession. Copy the BioSample accession (SAMN, SAMEA, or SAMD) from NCBI BioSample, or use the SRA accession of your reads (an SRR, ERR, or DRR run, an SRX experiment, or an SRS sample). For an SRA accession, RiboPilot finds its BioSample and also stores the run, experiment, study, platform, and library.

Full links work everywhere: RiboPilot trims them to the bare ID.

gbifIDs can change. GBIF may give an occurrence a new gbifID when its dataset is republished. If an ID stops working, RiboPilot keeps the data it fetched before and marks the fetch as failed. Look the specimen up again on gbif.org and paste the new ID.

title: Sample metadata: GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI
text:
Adding identifiers

At project setup
Add a column for any or all databases to your mapping file (see Your own project). Columns named GEOME_BCID, GBIF_ID, and BioSample (any upper or lower case) are found automatically. For other names, pass mapping_geome, mapping_gbif, and mapping_ncbi:
ID,Taxon,R1,R2,Tissue_BCID,Occurrence,SRA
Fish_01,Psenes pellucidus,Fish_01_R1.fastq.gz,Fish_01_R2.fastq.gz,ark:/21547/CXu2MBIO1000.1,,
Fish_02,Notemigonus crysoleucas,Fish_02_R1.fastq.gz,Fish_02_R2.fastq.gz,,6186461308,
Fish_03,Conger oceanicus,Fish_03_R1.fastq.gz,Fish_03_R2.fastq.gz,,,SRR21844202
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path          = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn    = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path     = "~/my_reads",
  mapping_geome = "Tissue_BCID",
  mapping_gbif  = "Occurrence",
  mapping_ncbi  = "SRA"
)

Blank cells are fine: those samples have no link.
Fetching needs internet access on the machine running R or the app. Offline, pass fetch_geome = FALSE, fetch_gbif = FALSE, and fetch_ncbi = FALSE, and fetch later. Pipeline jobs never contact these databases.

new_test_project() sets up the test project with linking on. Its fetch_metadata argument turns the NCBI fetch off.


Later
In the app, click the icon in the Metadata column, type or paste the ID, and click Fetch.
In R, add_samples() and update_sample_metadata() take the same mapping_*, fetch_*, and link_sources arguments. With update_sample_metadata(), samples whose ID changed or was added are fetched again, and a blank cell removes that sample’s link and data for that source only.
To fetch again without touching the mapping file:
RiboPilot::fetch_gbif("~/my_project")                   # every gbifID
RiboPilot::fetch_gbif("~/my_project", ids = "Fish_02")  # one sample
RiboPilot::fetch_gbif("~/my_project", ids = c("Fish_01", "Fish_02"),
                      gbifs = c("2336663130", "6186461308"))  # set new IDs, then fetch
RiboPilot::fetch_ncbi("~/my_project", ids = "Fish_03", ncbi_ids = "SAMN29555051")
RiboPilot::fetch_geome("~/my_project", ids = "Fish_01",
                       bcids = "ark:/21547/CXu2MBIO1000.1")
A blank ID removes the link. When some fetches fail, the rest still finish and a warning message lists each failed sample with the reason. A failed refresh keeps the data fetched before; changing to a different ID clears the old record right away. See the fetch messages table for additional details.
NCBI allows three requests per second, or ten with a free NCBI API key. Metadata fetches use the project’s ncbi_api_key or the NCBI_API_KEY/ENTREZ_KEY environment variables.

title: Sample metadata: GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI
text:
Viewing records in the app

The Metadata column
The Taxonomy, Assemble, Annotation Review, and Export tables have a Metadata column, with one logo per source the sample has an ID for:



Icon
Meaning




“+”
No IDs. Click it to add one.


GEOME “G”, GBIF leaf, NCBI helix
The record was fetched.


Faded logo
The ID is set but not fetched yet.


Faded logo with a warning triangle
The fetch failed. Hover to see why.


Orange flag
The sources disagree on at least one item (see Comparing sources).



Hovering over an icon lists each source with its status, then any items in conflict.


Showing metadata in the tables
The Metadata button above each table opens the Metadata fields window. It lists every field with a value for at least one sample: your mapping-file columns, then GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI fields, with an example value and a sample count (for example 12/20). Each row has two ticks:

Show adds the field as a column in the Taxonomy, Assemble, Annotation Review, and Export tables.
Export makes the field usable in FASTA header templates and writes it to the sample summary CSV.

Mapping-file columns start with Show ticked and are always available at export. Click Save to keep your choices in the project.


The sample metadata viewer
Click a sample’s Metadata icon to open the viewer. It has a tab for each database and a Compare tab. Here you can:

edit an ID and click Fetch (clear the box to remove the link),
click Refresh all to fetch every sample again,
filter fields by name, copy any value, or click Export CSV to save all of a sample’s metadata.

The Sample list on the left marks samples that failed to fetch or have a conflict. On the NCBI tab, records are shown as SRA, BioSample, and BioProject cards, each linked to its NCBI page.


Comparing sources
The Compare tab puts the values from your mapping file, GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI side by side for coordinates, collection date, country, locality, voucher, collector, sex, life stage, and taxon.







Status
Meaning




agree
Every source with a value agrees. Coordinates agree within 0.01 degree.


conflict
A real disagreement.


not checked
Free text, or a value that could not be read.


single
Only one source has a value.


-
No source has a value.



Blanks never conflict, and placeholders such as missing or not collected count as blank. RiboPilot finds your mapping-file columns by common names. If yours differ, pick them under Mapping file columns… at the bottom of the Compare tab, or in R:
RiboPilot::set_metadata_columns("~/my_project", country = "Country_Name",
                                coordinates = c("Lat_DD", "Long_DD"))
RiboPilot::set_metadata_columns("~/my_project", country = NA)  # back to automatic
RiboPilot::set_metadata_columns("~/my_project", sex = "")      # do not compare sex

title: Sample metadata: GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI
text:
Using metadata fields at export
A fetched value reaches your FASTA headers only after you tick Export for it in the Metadata button (see Showing metadata in the tables). Each source offers GenBank-ready fields, already formatted as GenBank source modifiers: the [name=value] tags in a FASTA header, such as [lat_lon=17.48 S 149.90 W]. The other fields are the raw values from each record. See GenBank submission for header templates and the modifiers GenBank requires.
In the Export Data window, the Available metadata panel lists every field you can use. Click one to insert it into the FASTA header box. A GenBank-ready field inserts the whole modifier, such as [lat_lon={gbif_lat_lon}]. Choose fields next to a source opens the Metadata fields window so you can enable more fields for export.
A template that takes every specimen value from GBIF:
{seqid} [organism={organism}] [moltype=genomic DNA] [lat_lon={gbif_lat_lon}] [collection_date={gbif_collection_date}] [geo_loc_name={gbif_geo_loc_name}] [specimen_voucher={gbif_specimen_voucher}] {organism} {rrna_definition}

Take a record’s values from one source where you can. Mixing sources can combine coordinates and dates from different collecting events. If you cite a BioSample with [BioSample=], GenBank expects the header values to agree with it.
Empty values are left out. A modifier with no value for a sample is dropped from that sample’s header instead of written empty, which GenBank rejects. The check under each header box names the records with empty modifiers, and warns when the same modifier appears twice. GenBank requires collection_date and geo_loc_name, so fill them in or use a missing-value term such as missing (see Required source modifiers).
Check GBIF values. GBIF’s country is its own English name (United   States of America, where GenBank expects USA), and GBIF may have adjusted or generalized coordinates. See the GBIF notes.
Your mapping file wins on a name clash. If your mapping file has a column with the same name as a ticked field (for example geome_lat_lon), its value is used in headers and the summary.

When you click Export, RiboPilot checks the items your templates use. If any sample in the export group has a conflict on one of them, the Sample metadata disagrees warning lists each sample, item, and value. Click Export anyway or Cancel.
NMNH specimens need two extra modifiers; see NMNH voucher submissions.

title: Sample metadata: GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI
text:
Removing fetched data
Remove fetched data… under the sample list in the viewer, or remove_metadata(), deletes fetched records for one sample or all:
RiboPilot::remove_metadata("~/my_project")                    # everything fetched
RiboPilot::remove_metadata("~/my_project", sources = "GBIF")  # one source
RiboPilot::remove_metadata("~/my_project", sources = c("GEOME", "GBIF"),
                           ids = "Fish_02")
This removes the stored records, their fetch status, and IDs that linking filled in. Your mapping-file columns, the IDs you supplied, and your field ticks are kept, so Refresh all or fetch_*() brings the data back.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
When a run ends with a failure, the app shows a report instead of the usual “Run finished with no failures.” The title says how the run ended: “Run finished with failures” (the run finished, but some samples or steps failed), “Run failed” (the run itself stopped with an error), or “Run stopped”.



A run report naming the failed sample and its likely cause, with the copy button


RiboPilot also saves every report in the project’s .runs/reports folder. Press Run Reports in the toolbar to see past runs, reference builds, and jobs submitted to a cluster, newest first. Here is a report from the test project, run on the full read sets (full_size = TRUE), where a second sample also fails:
RiboPilot run report
Project:   ~/ribopilot_test
Workflow:  pipeline, run peaceful_pare
Started:   2026-10-01 12:04:15
Finished:  2026-10-01 12:31:59 (27m 44s)
Result:    Finished with failures, exit status 0
Launched:  from the app
RiboPilot: 0.1.0
Nextflow:  25.10.6
Log:       ~/ribopilot_test/.runs/nextflow/pipeline_2026-10-01_12-04-14.nextflow.log
Tasks:     178 succeeded, 0 cached, 0 failed and skipped, 0 retried, 0 aborted
Samples:   12

Failed samples (sample | note | likely cause):
SRR14433899 | 11 or more paths exceed max_paths (10) | GetOrganelle found more alternative paths than Max paths allows.
SRR22396893 | 2 contig(s) under min_assembly_length (500 bp) | Every assembled contig was shorter than Min assembly length.
What each section means:

Workflow through Log: which workflow ran (the pipeline, a recheck, or a reference build), when, how it ended and with what exit status, whether it was started from the app or as a job, and where its full log is.
Tasks: how many pipeline steps ran, were reused from an earlier run, failed, were retried, or were stopped.
Failed tasks, when a step stopped with an error: one line per failed step, with the sample ID, the step (the pipeline step’s name; see the table below), the error code (the raw number the step exited with, for example 140), the likely cause, the last line of the step’s error output, and its working folder.
Failed samples: samples that finished without a usable assembly, with the pipeline’s note and the likely cause. After a recheck (Update on Annotation Review), Failed contigs lists instead each contig whose recheck failed or did not finish, with its note.

Samples that failed do not stop the others. Most steps skip a failed sample and carry on, so a run can finish with some samples done and a few failed.
The step names you may see, and what each step does:







Step
What it does




query_samples
Reads the list of samples to run from the project.


preprocess
Cleans and trims the reads.


below_min_depth
Marks samples with too few reads to assemble.


find_rrna_scan, find_rrna_pick, stage_assembly
Search an assembly you supplied for rDNA contigs.


assemble
Assembles the rDNA with GetOrganelle.


fallback_assemble
Assembles with SPAdes (baited or de-novo).


score
Scores the contigs and picks a path.


blast_genbank
Runs the BLAST screen: searches each contig in the bundled rDNA database, and at NCBI when that finds nothing.


blast_ref_fetch, blast_ref_align
Download reference sequences and align to them.


coverage
Maps the reads back for depth.


annotate_tools, reconcile
Find the five features.


curate, screen, chimera
Run the quality checks, the Screen verdict, and the chimera check.


triage
Proposes which contigs to keep.


query_recheck, recheck_tools, recheck
The recheck that Update on Annotation Review runs: pick the queued contigs, run barrnap and ITSx on each, then rerun its checks.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Error codes
These are the codes the report explains, with what they usually mean:








Code
What it usually means
What to do




104, 247
The step likely ran out of memory.
Raise Memory (GB) in that step’s options for the sample, for example in Assembly Options.


125
The container could not start: the image is missing, or a folder could not be mounted.
Check that Docker or Singularity works, and that the project’s image can be downloaded.


126
A command could not be run (permission denied).
Check the permissions of the project folder and the reads.


127
A command was not found: a tool is missing from the container or the PATH.
Usually the conda executor. Use Docker or Singularity.


130
The step was interrupted.
Press Update with Resume previous run? ticked.


134
The tool aborted, often because it ran out of memory.
Raise Memory (GB).


137
The step was killed: it ran out of memory, or the system stopped it.
Raise Memory (GB). On a cluster, it can also be a time limit: raise walltime in your profile.


139
The tool crashed (segmentation fault), often because it ran out of memory.
Raise Memory (GB).


140
The scheduler killed the job, usually because it went over its time or memory limit (SGE and LSF clusters).
More memory does not fix a time limit: raise walltime in your profile, or memory.


143
The step was stopped from outside, by the scheduler or by the system, often over its time or memory limit.
As for 140.


-
No exit code: the step was stopped before it finished.
Run again with Resume previous run? ticked.


any other
The tool stopped with an error.
Read the last error in the report, and the step’s log (see below).



The memory-hungry steps (preprocess, assemble, fallback_assemble, find_rrna_scan, annotate_tools, and recheck_tools) retry by themselves after codes 104, 134, 137, 139, 140, 143, and 247, up to three times, with more memory each time. The report says how often a step was tried.

title: Troubleshooting
section: When a sample fails for another reason
text:
When a sample fails for another reason
Some failures are not an error code: too few reads, only short contigs assembled, or no rRNA genes found. The Notes column says why, and the sample’s details window shows a red box with the reason and what to try next. To rescue a sample whose assembly failed, see the rescue section of the assemble walkthrough and choosing an assembly method.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Where to look

The run report, and the Notes column of the Assemble table.
The sample’s details window (click its ID).
Work Dirs, in the Assemble step: the pipeline’s working folder for each step of the ticked sample, with the step’s .command.log and .command.err.
Run Reports, in the toolbar: every run’s report.
The Nextflow log of each run, in the project’s .runs/nextflow folder.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Run a sample again
Select it, press State, choose Ready to run, then press Update with Resume previous run? ticked. Work that already finished is reused.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Stopping and resuming a run
Keep the browser tab open while a run is going. Closing the tab, reloading the page, closing the run window, or pressing Stop stops the run. RiboPilot stops it cleanly and keeps the work that finished. To carry on, press Update again with Resume previous run? ticked. Keep the computer awake too: a sleeping computer stops the run.
When you press Stop, the app says “Stopping the run: Nextflow is stopping its tasks. This can take up to a minute.” When it is done, a “Run stopped” report appears. If Nextflow does not stop within a minute, RiboPilot stops it by force, and the report says that some task containers may still be running: check them before you start a new run.
You can only spin up one run at a time for a project, and a stopped run still counts until its tasks have finished cleaning up. Pressing Update before then gives a message that a run is already going (see below).

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Common messages



Message
What it means
What to do




“database disk image is malformed”
The project database (.sqlite) is damaged.
Close the app and recover the database with the commands below this table, then open the app again.


“No samples to show. A sample is listed once its taxonomy is locked in the Taxonomy step. …”
The Assemble table lists only samples whose taxonomy is locked, and the Lock and State filters and the search box can hide the rest.
Lock the samples in the Taxonomy step, or reset the filters and clear the search box.


“Nothing to update”: “No samples or contigs are Ready to run. …”
Nothing is queued. Locked or finished samples are skipped.
Set the State of the rows you want to Ready to run, then press Update.


“N reference group(s) are not built or skipped (…).”
Some reference groups have no database yet. The run goes ahead, and those samples use the database their options already name.
Build the databases in the Reference step first.


“Cannot run: N reference database file(s) named by the samples queued for assembly are missing or empty (…).”
A database the samples point at is gone.
Rebuild it in the Reference step, or point those samples at a database that exists.


“A pipeline run is already going for this project, or is still stopping its tasks (started …).”
Another window, or a stopped run that is still cleaning up, holds the project.
Wait for it to finish, or stop it in the window that started it.


“The mapping file is missing column(s): …”
The mapping file needs ID, Taxon, R1, and R2 (or Assembly).
See Your own project.


“IDs may use only letters, digits, dash (-), underscore (_), and colon (:) …” or “IDs must be 40 characters or fewer.”
An ID breaks the ID rules.
Rename it in the mapping file.


“Read files named in the mapping file were not found in …”
A name in R1 or R2 does not match a file in data_path.
Check the spelling, and that names are relative to data_path.


“These paths have characters the pipeline cannot pass to Docker, Singularity, or Nextflow: …”
A path has a space, a quote mark, or another special character.
Rename it to use only letters, digits, and ., _, -, and /.


“Group name … cannot be used: it becomes a folder name …”
An export group name has a space or another special character.
Use the name the message suggests.


contaminant_unchecked, or the triage flag “BLAST screen has not run”
The BLAST screen has no usable hit for the contig: nothing matched in the bundled rDNA database, and the search at NCBI matched nothing, failed, or was switched off; or the bundled database returned a hit whose lineage could not be resolved, so the contig was never sent on to NCBI. It also appears when the sample has no taxon.
If NCBI could not be reached, set the sample to Ready to run and press Update once it can: the contig is searched again. For a bundled-database hit with no usable lineage, choose “NCBI only (core_nt)” under Search in the sample’s BLAST Options, then set it Ready to run and press Update. If the sample has no taxon, set one in the Taxonomy step.


“Nextflow … is below the minimum supported version (24.10.0).”
Your Nextflow is too old.
Install Nextflow 24.10 through 25.10; see Installation.


“Nextflow … is newer than RiboPilot has verified … Runs will be pinned to Nextflow 25.10.6 via NXF_VER.”
RiboPilot runs a supported version instead, downloading it once.
Nothing, or install a supported version.


“Container image … is not published on Docker Hub, so container executors will fail at image pull.”
The project names an image Docker cannot download.
Check the container you passed to new_project(), and your network.


“Container version does not match RiboPilot” (when the app opens)
The project’s .config names the RiboPilot image for another version, so runs use that image’s code and tools.
Run RiboPilot::backwards_compatibility() on the project (see Upgrading). The app works either way.



To recover a damaged project database, run these in the project folder:
mv .sqlite .sqlite_corrupted
sqlite3 .sqlite_corrupted ".recover" | sqlite3 .sqlite

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Asking for help
Open an issue at https://github.com/NMNH-OceanDNA/RiboPilot/issues. Paste the copied run report, and add your RiboPilot version (packageVersion("RiboPilot") in R), your Nextflow version (nextflow -v), and whether you use Docker, Singularity, or a cluster profile. Check that nothing you paste contains your NCBI API key.

title: Quality checks and flags
text:
After RiboPilot annotates a contig (see Get started), it runs a set of automatic quality checks and raises a curation warning for anything that looks unusual. Warnings never change your assemblies or annotations. They flag something that may need your attention.
You can find the results in three places:
Below is a list of all the checks and warnings columns you will see in the app:
This page explains the Checks column first, then each family of checks in turn, and ends with the per-group length and identity tables.

title: Quality checks and flags
text:
The Checks column
The Checks column puts every check on one line, worst first, in a color that matches the worst finding. On the Assemble table it summarizes all of the sample’s kept contigs.








Checks says
Color
What happens




off target, contaminant, severe chimera, or ITSx chimeric
red
Lock and the Export window ask first, until the contig is marked Reviewed.


minor chimera, uncertain screen, ITSx, ITSx not checked, warnings, or feature flags
amber
Worth a look, but nothing asks when you Lock or Export.


ok
green
The best BLAST matches are in your sample’s phylum, and nothing is flagged.


no reference
gray
Nothing is flagged, but the BLAST screen had no usable match to judge by.



A red finding does not stop you, but locking or exporting that sample will ask you to confirm. Setting a problematic sample as Mark Reviewed will override those prompts on lock or export (see Annotation Review).

title: Quality checks and flags
text:
Curation warnings
In the Annotation Review module, these are the warning codes counted by the Warnings column and reported in the Curation warnings panel when you examine a contig in detail.



Warning
Level
What it means
What to do




missing_18S, missing_5.8S, missing_28S
contig
One of the three rRNA genes was not found.

title: Quality checks and flags
text:
The BLAST screen and auto-triage
Every contig is run through a BLAST search once it is assembled. The result feeds the Screen column, the contamination warnings above, the chimera check, and the triage rules below, which propose whether to keep or drop the contig.

What the screen searches
By default each contig is searched against the bundled rDNA database inside the container: about 600,000 animal nuclear rDNA records from GenBank. This database also includes NCBI’s 16S, eukaryote small subunit, and eukaryote large subunit rRNA sets so that a contaminant bacterial, fungal, or plant contig still finds a match. Contigs that match nothing in the bundled database are searched against the NCBI nucleotide database (core_nt) over the internet.
To change how the BLAST search works, open a sample’s BLAST Options in the Assemble module and pick a Search choice: “Bundled database only” never goes to NCBI, and “NCBI only (core_nt)” skips the bundled database.
In Annotation Review, the Hit Source column says which database was used to determine the contig’s best BLAST hit: “bundled”, “NCBI”, or “seed file” (the assembly’s own seed database, which is only a hint).


How contigs are kept or dropped
Once a contig has been screened, RiboPilot checks the eight rules below in order and proposes to keep or drop the contig. For rules whose action is Flag, the contig status stays undecided and the Why column in the sample’s contig table gives the reason. You can override any call by hand with the K (keep) and D (drop) buttons in the Assemble details window.









#
Rule
What it means
Default action




1
Annotation has not run
Neither annotation tool has reported on this contig yet.
Flag only


2
BLAST screen has not run
No usable BLAST hit is recorded, or the only matches are whole-genome assemblies, so the contig cannot be judged. Also raises contaminant_unchecked.
Flag only


3
No annotations, non-rDNA hit
Annotation found no rRNA or ITS feature, and the best match is not a nuclear rDNA record.
Drop


4
No annotations but rDNA hit
Annotation found no rRNA or ITS feature, but the best match is a nuclear rDNA record.
Flag (can be set to Drop)


5
Has annotations but non-rDNA hit
The contig has an rRNA or ITS feature, but the best match is not a nuclear rDNA record.
Flag (can be set to Drop)


6
GenBank taxonomy disagrees with the sample
The contig’s BLAST hits agree on a taxon outside your sample’s phylum. This is the contaminant warning.
Flag (can be set to Drop)


7
Disagrees with sibling contigs
This contig’s top hit disagrees with the majority of this sample’s other contigs. A hint, not proof.
Flag only


8
Chimeric assembly (severe)
Parts of this contig match organisms from different phyla or kingdoms.
Flag only



Rule 6 compares at phylum rank. It catches a fungal, bacterial, or plant contaminant, but cannot separate two organisms in the same phylum.
To change what a rule does to a contig, select samples in the Assemble table and click the Triage button at the top. The Triage window lets you set each rule to Off, Flag, or Drop, shows how many contigs each rule would decide, and reruns triage for the selected samples when you click Apply.

title: Quality checks and flags
text:
Chimeric contigs
A chimera is one assembled contig containing sequences that do not belong together, such as rDNA from two organisms or two different copies of the repeat from one genome. Each contig gets a chimera level, shown in the Chimera column of Annotation Review and in the Checks column:









Level
What it means
Triage
Export




severe
Two parts of the contig match different phyla or kingdoms, each at 90 percent identity or more.
Rule 8 flags the contig.
Red in Checks. The submission_risk column says chimeric(...).


minor
Weaker evidence: windows match more than one class, genes agree only at a high rank, a ribotyper warning, or read evidence alone.
No rule fires.
Amber in Checks. Listed in the chimera_warning column of the summary CSV; not a submission risk.


clean
Nothing found.
No rule fires.
Nothing.



In the test project, CHIM01 is severe: the contig is an artificial chimera composed of sequence from ray-finned fish and Penicillium mold.



A real chimera in the sequence viewer: the origin track switches lineage at the junction



How the check works
RiboPilot looks for chimeras in four ways:

Gene by gene. The 18S, 5.8S, and 28S genes each get their own best GenBank matches. Ideally these agree on one lineage.
Along the contig. The contig is divided into 150 bp windows and each is searched against the bundled rDNA database. Neighboring windows that match the same taxonomic class are joined into segments, and neighboring segments that hit different classes suggest a chimeric join. Neighboring segments with different taxonomic assignment are only flagged when both segments span at least 450 bp (for class mismatches) or 300 bp (for phylum or kingdom mismatches).
Gene structure. ribotyper, NCBI’s rRNA checker, tests that the 18S and 28S each look like one whole gene. ITSx’s own chimera call adds a little weight.
Reads. Many mapped reads that stop at the same point, or a large shift in read depth, can indicate a chimeric join.



How to judge a flag
In the Coverage and windowed BLAST panel:

Window BLAST taxon shows segments with consistent taxonomic identity
Window BLAST identity shows the best hit’s percent identity
vertical red dashed lines mark possible chimeric junctions

The Windowed BLAST details panel below provides more details about the BLAST results.
A real chimera shows a clean switch from one lineage to another, often accompanied by a shift in read depth. RiboPilot already discounts the common false positives: windows in conserved stretches where many groups match equally well are shown as “unresolved” and changes in read depth at a gene boundary or at the ends of the contig are ignored. Below, the first contig of SRR33849683 is “minor” because its genes agree only at phylum level, although every window that can be placed matches a ray-finned fish:



Windowed BLAST details for a weaker signal that needs a look


If in doubt, copy the contig with Copy FASTA and run your own BLAST searches on the NCBI website.

title: Quality checks and flags
section: Feature BLAST: each feature searched on its own
text:
Feature BLAST: each feature searched on its own
The contig BLAST search can look fine even if one feature is poorly assembled or contaminated. So RiboPilot also searches each core feature (18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 28S) on its own against the bundled rDNA database.
The Feature BLAST warnings column in Annotation Review lists only the features that need a look:







Warning
Meaning




no hit
Nothing in the database matched the feature.


non-rDNA hit
The best match is not a nuclear rDNA record.


off-target (group)
The best match shares nothing with your sample at phylum level or below.


no BLAST, feature too small
The feature is under 50 bp, too short for a useful search. Features of 50 to 99 bp are searched but marked low confidence, because short pieces match many organisms equally well.


weak hit
Only the more sensitive dc-megablast retry found a match; megablast found nothing.



In the Annotation Review table, open a contig Details window to see the full Feature BLAST panel. This shows each feature’s best match, how closely it matches your sample (species, genus, family, and so on), its identity and coverage, and the algorithm that found it (megablast, dc-megablast in amber, or blastn for short features). Expand a row for the top 10 matches. “Not run” means the database was not available.
In the test project, CHIM01’s 28S comes from a Penicillium mold, so its best match shares nothing with the fish sample and the feature is off target:



Feature BLAST for CHIM01: the 18S matches the fish, the 28S is off target

title: Quality checks and flags
text:
Several contigs from one organism
When a sample assembles more than one rDNA contig, RiboPilot compares their 18S, 5.8S, and 28S genes. The result is shown in the Variant column of the Assemble step’s contig table. Too little shared gene sequence gives “not comparable”.
An isomer is RiboPilot’s label for contigs whose rRNA genes are nearly identical but which differ in the ITS sequence or flanking regions.
A paralog means the genes of the contigs differ. That can be real variation within one genome (known in octocorals and jellyfish), contamination, or a pseudogene.
A contaminant from the same phylum passes the contig screen, so check each variant’s Feature BLAST warnings before you lock one. Handle isomers and paralogs with care: consult the literature for your group, or examine a reference genome, to see whether rDNA variation is a known phenomenon.

title: Quality checks and flags
section: How the checks are tuned per group
text:
How the checks are tuned per group
The expected lengths and identity floors depend on the group of organisms. RiboPilot ships five rulesets, with ranges taken from GenBank records:

The floors are lower for sea stars, jellyfish, and octocorals because GenBank has fewer rDNA records for these groups. All of these are working values, not published standards: a length or low_identity warning is a prompt to look, not a verdict. In every ruleset, a gene is truncated when less than 90 percent of its rRNA model was recovered, identity is judged only when the reference covers at least half of the gene, and annotation gaps of 5 bases or fewer are closed automatically.
Want ranges for your own group? Open an issue describing it. Until then, the generic animal ruleset works for any group; it is just more lenient.

title: Your own project
text: A project starts with a mapping file that lists your samples, and one command that sets up the project folder. After that, everything happens in the app, the same way as in Get started.

title: Your own project
text:
The mapping file
The mapping file is a CSV file with one row per sample. For example:
ID,Taxon,R1,R2,Voucher
Fish_01,Brosme brosme,Fish_01_R1.fastq.gz,Fish_01_R2.fastq.gz,USNM 123456
Fish_02,Upeneus parvus,SRR22396758/SRR22396758_1.fastq.gz,SRR22396758/SRR22396758_2.fastq.gz,USNM 123457
Snail_01,Tritia reticulata,Snail_01_R1.fq.gz,Snail_01_R2.fq.gz,
The rules:

Columns. It needs the columns ID, Taxon, R1, and R2. Upper and lower case do not matter in column names.
Taxon. Give the species name whenever you can (for example Upeneus parvus), spelled as NCBI has it; a genus or higher group works when the species is unknown. RiboPilot uses it to pick the reference database and the quality checks, to judge contamination, and as the organism name in your GenBank records.
IDs. Each ID must be unique, ignoring case, and at most 40 characters long. Use only letters, digits, dash (-), underscore (_), and colon (:): no spaces, dots, or slashes.
Commas only. Save the file with commas between values. From Excel, use File > Save As > CSV UTF-8 (Comma delimited).
Paired reads only. Every sample with Illumina reads needs both an R1 and an R2 file. Single-end reads are not currently supported.
Read file names are relative to the read folder you pass as data_path. Subfolders are fine (SRR22396758/SRR22396758_1.fastq.gz), but full paths are not.
No spaces or special characters in paths. File names, folder names, and the project path may use only letters, digits, and ., _, -, and /. RiboPilot stops and names each path it cannot pass to Docker, Singularity, or Nextflow, for example one with a space or a quote mark.
Extra columns are kept, and you can use them in your GenBank headers, for example as {Voucher}. A column name with a space or a dash is read with a dot in its place, so Voucher ID becomes {Voucher.ID}. The Your mapping columns chips in the Export window show every name.
Metadata ID columns. Columns named GEOME_BCID, GBIF_ID, and BioSample hold a sample’s GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI identifiers. RiboPilot fetches those records when it sets up the project. Blank cells are fine. To use other column names, pass mapping_geome, mapping_gbif, or mapping_ncbi to the new_project() function. See Sample metadata.
Reserved names. RiboPilot adds some columns itself, so your file cannot use these names: taxid, sci_name, rank, match_type, tax_alternatives, lineage, lineage_taxids, ref_id, user_group, ref_source, taxonomy_switch, taxonomy_lock, and time_stamp.

The IDs end up in your GenBank records, so choose them with care.

title: Your own project
text:
Create the project
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path       = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads"
)
RiboPilot checks the mapping file and the read files before it writes anything, and stops with an error message if it encounters any issues.
By default, new_project() assumes you are running RiboPilot on a local workstation (i.e. a desktop or laptop). For projects on a computing cluster, pass your cluster profile as executor; see Running on a cluster.
An NCBI API key is optional; see Installation for where to put it.
Once the project is created, open the app and follow the five steps, as in Get started.
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("~/my_project")
Run a handful of samples through every step before you run hundreds: settings that are wrong for your group are much cheaper to find on a small run. Make sure to do the Reference step before running the Assemble workflow.

title: Your own project
text:
Already have an assembly?
If you have a genome assembly for a sample, or just the contig that contains the ribosomal repeat, you can use it instead of assembling from reads. Add an Assembly column to your mapping file naming that sample’s FASTA file, and pass the folder that holds them as assembly_path:
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path          = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn    = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path     = "~/my_reads",
  assembly_path = "~/my_assemblies"
)
The assembly files must be FASTA files, all gzipped (.gz) or all uncompressed in one project, and named relative to assembly_path.
RiboPilot searches each supplied assembly for rRNA genes and carries forward the contigs that carry an 18S or 28S anchor. A single ribosomal contig passes this search without doing anything special. If you supplied a fragment too short to carry an anchor (an ITS-only sequence, for example), turn the search off in the app’s Assembly Options and RiboPilot uses your file exactly as given.
A sample with an assembly does not need reads: leave R1 and R2 blank in the mapfile. If your file has no reads at all, you can leave out the R1 and R2 columns and data_path entirely. A sample with no reads gets no depth profile, since there is nothing to map back.

title: Your own project
text:
Adding samples later
To add samples to a project you have already started, write a mapping file that lists only the new samples, and run:
RiboPilot::add_samples(
  "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/more_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads"
)
It runs the same checks as new_project(), and refuses IDs that are already in the project. Put the new read files in the same folder as the project’s other reads (the data_path you gave new_project()). The new samples then appear in the Taxonomy step, ready to assign.
To fix or add metadata, such as a voucher number, for samples that are already in the project, list them in a mapping file with the new values and run RiboPilot::update_sample_metadata() the same way. It never changes a sample’s reads, assembly, state, or locks.
Do not rerun new_project() with force = TRUE on a project you have worked on: it deletes all existing results.

title: Your own project
section: What is in the project folder
text:
What is in the project folder
The project folder holds your results database, its settings, and the pipeline’s working files. The table in Disk space, caches, and offline use says what each item is and when you can safely delete them.

title: Test project: Annotation Review
text:
Test project: 0. Get started 1. Taxonomy 2. Reference 3. Assemble 4. Annotation Review 5. Export
For the test project, do this:
Contigs must be locked here before they can be exported. The rest of this page explains what you are looking at.
Each kept contig of a locked sample is one row:
The Checks column summarizes the checks for each contig. The Warnings, ITSx Warnings, Screen, Chimera, and Feature BLAST warnings columns show a breakdown of each contig check.
Quality checks and flags explains what each warning means.

title: Test project: Annotation Review
text:
Examining contig details
Click a contig’s ID to see more details.



A contig: its five features, read coverage, and gene map


At the top of this window, two buttons record what you decided about a contig: Mark Reviewed and Exclude & Lock. A badge beside them shows whether the contig is complete or partial.
Lock locks the contig and keeps the window open; Lock & Close locks it and closes the window. Neither marks it Reviewed. If the contig failed some of the checks and is not marked Reviewed, RiboPilot will print warning messages when you attempt to lock the sample.
A locked contig is read only. To make any edits, unlock it first. Only contigs that are locked can be exported. Only one assembly path can be locked per sample: paths are alternative reconstructions of the same rDNA repeat, so a sample should only export one. However, multiple contigs can be locked and exported for the same sample.
Below that is a table of annotated features (18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 28S).
Next is the Coverage and windowed BLAST panel, which draws the contig as an interactive plot. The plot contains several tracks: read depth, the percentage of clipped reads, the features (arrows indicate orientation, dashed ends are partial annotations), the base pairs (once you zoom in), and the chimera check’s window BLAST identity and taxon tracks. Scroll to zoom, drag to pan, or type a position. Clicking a gene makes it the active feature that will show up in the Edit active feature boundaries and the Reference alignment panels below.

title: Test project: Annotation Review
text:
Trimming the contig
GenBank tends to reject submissions containing sequence outside the core 18s-5.8s-28s region. So for a real submission, it is best to trim your contigs before export.
To trim many contigs at once, tick them in the Annotate Details table and press Trim in the toolbar. Choose Match gene ends to keep only the annotated span, or Gene ends + flank to keep a few extra bases on each side. Only contigs with all five features (18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, and 28S) can be trimmed using this bulk trim button.
To trim partial contigs, open the details window and click Trim assembly. The window plots read depth with the features colored and the kept range marked. Choose Annotated feature boundaries, Annotated + flank, or Custom range, where you can type the range or drag across the plot to set it.



The Trim assembly window for one contig, set to keep the annotated span


RiboPilot always saves the original contig, so you can use the Restore button (or Restore assembly in a contig details window) to undo a trim. Restore returns the contig to its original sequence, features, and check results: it undoes every trim, gene boundary edit, and 5’/3’ choice on the contig. Your Reviewed and Exclude marks, notes, and export group stay as they are.

title: Test project: Annotation Review
text:
Editing feature boundaries
The Edit active feature boundaries and Reference alignment panels can be used to modify the boundaries of the selected feature. First, click a row in the feature table, or a gene arrow in the viewer, to select that feature. Then open these panels to make adjustments. All other figures will be updated whenever you adjust an annotation.



Editing the 5.8S boundaries, with the feature aligned against its reference hits below


Tick Edit to show the controls. Step (nt) sets how many bases each click moves a boundary, from 1 to 50. Under 5’ end and 3’ end, + extends the feature outward and - trims it inward. The Partial buttons allow you to manually mark the 5’ or 3’ end as partial, which will be reflected in the exported files.
Each time you edit a feature, the feature table, the sequence viewer, and the reference alignment will update. Press Save to keep the edit, or Reset to put the boundaries back. Moving one feature’s boundary does not adjust its neighbor, so a gap or overlap between them shows up as a warning after the next Update.
Reference alignment aligns the active feature against its top BLAST hits. Use the alignment to check that your feature is consistent with other published sequences. The panel is empty when the pipeline found no reference hits for the feature.

title: Test project: Annotation Review
text:
Updating checks after edits
After a trim or an edit to gene boundaries, the contig’s checks are marked “not run”. Trims and edits modify a working copy of the contig, so the original remains untouched. Until the checks are run again, the contig’s State shows Ready to run, and its check columns and Checks say “not run”.
To rerun the checks, press Update in the Annotation Review toolbar, then Run from App (on a cluster, the window offers a job script, as in the Assemble step).

title: Test project: Annotation Review
text:
Locking contigs when done
Only locked contigs reach the Export step, so lock each contig once you are happy with it. Tick the rows and press Lock in the toolbar, or use Lock or Lock & Close in a contig’s details window. The same button unlocks a locked contig.
Lock checks a few things first:

Every selected contig’s checks must be done. If any show “not run”, nothing is locked, and a message lists those contigs with “Press Update first.”
Only one assembly path can be locked per sample. Paths are alternative reconstructions of the same rDNA repeat, so a sample should only export one. Several contigs of the same path can be locked together.
A contig flagged by the BLAST screen or the chimera check prompts a warning message. . Choose Lock anyway to continue. The Export window asks about it again unless you mark it Reviewed.




Lock asks about a flagged contig that is not marked Reviewed


A locked contig is read only. To trim it or move a boundary, unlock it first. To keep a contig out of the export altogether, use Exclude & Lock.
For the test project, tick every row, press Lock, and choose Lock anyway for CHIM01.

Next: Export →

title: Test project: Taxonomy
text:
Test project: 0. Get started 1. Taxonomy 2. Reference 3. Assemble 4. Annotation Review 5. Export

This walkthrough picks up where Get started leaves off.
By clicking Assign Taxonomy, RiboPilot matches each Taxon in your mapping file to the NCBI taxonomy database. The first time this runs, it downloads about 80 MB and builds an index of about 0.5 GB inside the project, which takes a few minutes.
The Confidence column says how well your taxon names matched the NCBI taxonomy database:








Confidence
What it means
What to do

Your taxon name matched exactly one NCBI taxon.
Nothing.

No exact match, so a species of the same genus with a very similar name was picked.
Check the spelling.

Only the genus matched.
Check the name, and pick the species if NCBI has it.

The name matches more than one organism; for example, the genus Morus is both a mulberry and a gannet. No taxon is set.
Pick the right one. The Other Matches column lists each candidate with its kingdom.

In the test project, all 12 test samples match exactly:



Taxonomy step with all 12 test samples matched and locked



Next: Reference →

title: Linking records across databases
text: GEOME, GBIF, and NCBI records often point to each other. With linking on, one ID per sample is enough: from a column of SRA accessions, for example, RiboPilot can also find and fetch the matching GEOME and GBIF records. This page builds on Sample metadata.

title: Linking records across databases
text:
Turning linking on
Linking is off by default, because it makes extra requests and fills in IDs you did not type. Turn it on for a project at setup, or for one fetch:
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path         = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn   = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path    = "~/my_reads",
  link_sources = TRUE
)
RiboPilot::fetch_ncbi("~/my_project", link_sources = TRUE)  # this fetch only
In the app, tick Follow links between databases next to Fetch in the sample metadata viewer. The setting is saved in the project, and later fetch_*() calls follow it unless you pass link_sources.

text:
How RiboPilot links database records



How RiboPilot links records across databases. Each arrow reads the record at its tail and fills in the ID at its head.





From

Rules that keep linking safe:

Your IDs always win. RiboPilot only fills a database when the sample has no ID for it. If a record points elsewhere, yours is kept and the viewer notes “… record links to …; kept your ID …”.
The first link wins. Records are read in the order GEOME, GBIF, NCBI. If two databases link to different records in the third, the first is linked and the other is noted.
Each database is fetched at most once per sample, so links cannot loop.
Every linked ID says where it came from, for example “Found through NCBI BioSample voucherURI” in the viewer.


Sequencing runs can differ. GEOME may name a different SRA run than the one you assembled, for example when a tissue was sequenced twice. RiboPilot links by BioSample, which both runs share.

title: Linking records across databases
section: Matching a voucher to a GBIF record
text:
Matching a voucher to a GBIF record
Only Smithsonian specimens carry an EZID that points straight at a GBIF record. For other museums, RiboPilot searches GBIF for the specimen voucher, written as GenBank and museums write it (the Darwin Core forms): institution:collection:catalog (USNM:FISH:419933), institution:catalog (UW:157636), either with a urn:catalog: prefix, or institution catalog (USNM 419933). It searches the fields listed in the field reference, filters the hits, and links only when exactly one specimen is left:



How a voucher is matched to one GBIF record



The species must match. One catalog number can belong to many specimens. A genus-only Taxon matches by genus.
The collection code narrows, but does not reject. A single match under another code is kept, since GenBank and GBIF often name collections differently.
Copies are skipped. GBIF occurrences copied from GenBank or the Barcode of Life are ignored; they are not museum records.

Vouchers without an institution code or specimens the museum has not published to GBIF cannot be matched.

title: Linking records across databases
section: Why is my sample not linked?
text:
Why is my sample not linked?

Is linking on? It is off by default; see Turning linking on.
Did the sample already have an ID for that database? Your IDs are never replaced. Look for “kept your ID” in the viewer.
Did the voucher match several GBIF specimens? The viewer says “N possible GBIF matches for …; not linked”, or “too many GBIF matches” for more than 50. Paste the right gbifID.
Does the record carry a link at all? Open it in the viewer and check the fields in the table above. Many records name no other database.
Did the linked fetch fail? Hover the faded logo in the Metadata column, or see the fetch messages.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
text: RiboPilot writes one folder per export group containing everything you need to submit your records to GenBank: the sequences (with customized FASTA headers), feature tables, and a summary of the checks. This page helps you understand the GenBank submission process. The Export walkthrough shows the Export step itself.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
text:
Which files to upload
For rRNA and ITS sequences, NCBI’s Submission Portal (https://submit.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) takes a FASTA file only. Upload <group>.fasta. The Portal finds the genes itself with ITSx, and writes its own annotation, so the .tbl feature tables are not used there.
The Portal rewrites definition lines in its own wording (small and large subunit ribosomal RNA), so the 18S and 28S wording in your file will not survive.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
Preparing a GenBank submission
text:
Required source modifiers
For each rDNA sequences, GenBank requires the organism name, one identifier for the sample (isolate, strain, clone, or specimen voucher), the collection date, and where it was collected. Add them to your template as source modifiers: [specimen_voucher=...], [collection_date=...], and [geo_loc_name=...]. NCBI’s full list is Modifiers for FASTA Definition Lines.
For example, with Voucher, Date, and Country columns in your mapping file:
{seqid} [organism={organism}] [specimen_voucher={Voucher}] [collection_date={Date}] [geo_loc_name={Country}] [moltype=genomic DNA] {organism} {rrna_definition}
Instead of including these values as columns in your mapping file, you can fetch them from GEOME, GBIF, or NCBI BioSample. The Export column of the Metadata button offers ready-made values such as {geome_lat_lon} and {gbif_collection_date}, which you place in the template yourself. Smithsonian NMNH specimens also need a voucherURI; see NMNH voucher submissions.
If a record would get an empty modifier, such as [collection_date=] for a sample with no date, the template check warns and names the records. NCBI does not accept an empty modifier: fill in the column, or use one of NCBI’s accepted missing-value terms, such as missing or not collected. If you continue with export, missing metadata in the FASTA header will be removed on a sample-by-sample basis.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
text:
The organism name
{organism} is the name confirmed in the Taxonomy step. If the Taxonomy step did not result in an exact match, {organism} is set to the Taxon label from your map file, so an informal name such as “Upeneus sp. A” is kept. To always use your own label, put {Taxon} in the template instead.
When your map file Taxon differs from the name set in the Taxonomy step, the record’s submission_risk column says taxon_differs(<name>), so you can check which one you want.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
section: Samples with more than one record
text:
Samples with more than one record
When a sample has more than one contig at export, RiboPilot adds [isolate=<ID>_p<path>_s<contig>] to each FASTA header. This allows GenBank to differentiate records that share an organism and a voucher number.
For that reason, a template with its own [isolate=...] is refused for an export group that contains a sample with multiple contigs. It is allowed otherwise.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
text:
Complete or partial
Since GenBank performs its own annotation, the following information can usually be ignored for the submission process.
The end of a gene is written as partial (< for the 5’ end or > for the 3’ end in the feature table, and “partial sequence” in the definition line) when:

it runs into the end of a contig that has not been trimmed (the gene ran off the assembled contig)
the quality check found the gene truncated, meaning less than 90 percent of it was recovered. The end that meets no neighboring spacer or gene is marked if both ends meet one, both are marked
a trim cut through the gene. A trim that lands on a gene boundary marks nothing

Your own choice always wins: the 5’ and 3’ buttons under Partial in the contig window (check Edit, pick the feature, then Save) can be used to override RiboPilot. The Completeness column in the Annotate table reads “complete” only when all five features are present and no gene end is partial.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
text:
Flanking sequence
Contigs often contain sequence beyond the core rDNA region. This is intergenic spacer (IGS): 5’ external transcribed spacer (ETS) before the 18S, and its 3’ ETS after the 28S. RiboPilot does not annotate these flanks, and GenBank tends to reject submissions containing sequences containing IGS/ETS. We recommend that you trim contigs to gene boundaries before export.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
text:
Gaps inside a record
A run of 10 or more N bases counts as a gap. NCBI may remove a record with a gap inside the 18S-to-28S region; the gap_in_rDNA flag below marks these.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
text:
Check before you submit
After export, the summary files note samples that have submission-risk flags. However, some warning messages may also appear during the export process.
Flagged records. Before it writes anything, the Export window lists every contig that the BLAST screen or the chimera check flagged, and that you have not marked “Reviewed”. You can choose to Leave them out or Export anyway.
The ITSx check. NCBI runs a standard ITSx check on every rRNA and ITS submission. It may suggest that you remove records judged chimeric, gapped, or misassembled by ITSx. RiboPilot runs the same stock ITSx check on every contig when it annotates it, and again when Update on Annotation Review rechecks a contig you trimmed or edited. Export does not run ITSx: it reports the stored result in the itsx_check column of <group>_summary.csv, and the Export done window counts the flagged, clean, and not checked records and names the flagged ones. The ITSx Warnings column in the app shows the same flags. It only warns: nothing is removed.
RiboPilot checks one contig at a time, while NCBI runs ITSx on your whole upload at once. ITSx’s calls can shift a little with the set of sequences it is given, so on borderline records NCBI’s check may differ from RiboPilot’s.
An itsx_check value that starts with not_run means ITSx gave no answer for that record. The record still counts as checked, so it can be locked and exported, and NCBI checks it again when you upload. To check it again in RiboPilot, unlock the contig in Annotation Review, set its State to Ready to run, press Update, and lock it again once its checks are finished.







Value
What it means




not_run(ITSx did not finish)
ITSx crashed or was stopped before it finished this contig.


not_run(ITSx check failed: <message>)
Reading the ITSx result failed; the message says why.


not_run(not checked before upgrade)
The contig was locked in an older RiboPilot version that stored no ITSx check for it.


not_run(not checked)
No ITSx check is stored for the record.


any other not_run(...)
Stored by an older RiboPilot version, for example not_run(no ITSx output).



The GenBank BLAST check. Before assigning accessions, GenBank’s rRNA/ITS curation searches each record (default megablast) against NCBI’s ITS_eukaryote_sequences database and its eukaryote SSU/LSU rRNA database. It sends a submission back for review when the top hit:

covers under 75% of the record (“Query coverage is less than 75%”), or
aligns to it in more than one piece (“HSP_problem”, a potential misassembly).

RiboPilot runs the same two searches on each contig when it annotates it, and again when Update rechecks a trimmed or edited contig. The result appears in:

the GenBank BLAST column of the app,
the Export done window, which names the flagged records,
the genbank_check column of <group>_summary.csv, and
README.txt.

It only warns. Nothing is removed, and nothing is gated on it.
Expect these flags on most fish records, and on other groups the ITS database covers thinly. The database holds a few hundred fish records among 77,000 plant and fungal ones, so the top hit is a distant relative, the ITS spacers do not align to it, and the record splits into an 18S piece and a 5.8S piece. That is not evidence of a bad assembly. NCBI’s copy of the database is newer than the one RiboPilot ships, so a record near 75% can be called differently.







Value
What it means




genbank_low_coverage(ITS <n>%)
The top hit in the ITS database covers under 75% of the record.


genbank_multi_hsp(<db> <n> HSPs: ...)
The top hit in that database aligns in more than one piece; the positions on the record follow.


genbank_no_hit(<db>)
No hit at all in that database.


not_run(no ITS_eukaryote_sequences database)
The installed panel predates the release that ships the ITS database. Install a newer panel with install_ribopilot_db() (or pull a newer image), then run the contig’s checks again.


any other not_run(...)
blastn failed or the contig has no sequence; run its checks again as described for the ITSx check.



The submission_risk column. Each record’s row in <group>_summary.csv lists any of these flags:







Flag
What it means




chimeric(...)
Parts of the sequence match different phyla or kingdoms (a severe chimera call); the reason is in brackets.


chimeric(ITSx)
ITSx calls the record chimeric.


gap_in_rDNA
A run of N bases falls between the start of the 18S and the end of the 28S.


misassembly
Features overlap or are out of order.


off_target(<taxon>)
The BLAST screen’s hits agree on a taxon that is not on the sample’s lineage.


contaminant
The BLAST screen’s best hit is from a different phylum than the sample.


taxon_differs(<name>)
Your Taxon differs from the name set in the Taxonomy step.


missing_organism
The record has no organism name.



Check off_target and contaminant records before you submit: the sequence may be another organism’s rDNA, exported under your sample’s name. Weaker chimera evidence is in the separate chimera_warning column; it is not a submission risk, but it is worth a look in the app.

title: Preparing a GenBank submission
section: What is in the export folder
text:
What is in the export folder
out/export/<group>/
    <group>.fasta           every record, one file (this is what you upload)
    <group>.tbl             feature tables (for your records; not uploaded)
    <group>_summary.csv     one row per record, with submission_risk
    <group>_report.html     review report with feature maps and alignments
    README.txt              how to submit
    samples/                one .fasta and .tbl per record
    markers/                one folder per marker (18S, ITS1, and so on)
The summary CSV also says which records are variants of each other, in the variant_class, variant_group, variant_identity, and n_variants columns; see Quality checks and flags.

title: Installation
text:
RiboPilot runs its analysis inside a container: Docker on a workstation, or Singularity (also called Apptainer) on a computing cluster. The container holds every analysis tool, so you do not install them yourself.
RiboPilot is developed and tested on Linux. On a Mac it needs Docker Desktop. On Windows, use WSL2 and run R inside WSL. On a cluster, use Singularity or Apptainer (see Running on a cluster).
Disk space. The container image is about 2.6 GB to download and 7.7 GB on disk. Each project also needs room for its own files: the test project used 1.6 GB, mostly Nextflow’s working files (0.9 GB) and the taxonomy copy (0.5 GB). Reference databases are small: the two built for the test project took 4 MB and 16 MB. Disk space, caches, and offline use says where each of these goes, and how to move it.
