title: Installation
text:
Install the tools
Install each of these once, and check it with the command beside it.

Docker (workstation). On Linux, add yourself to the docker group so Docker runs without sudo. On a Mac, start Docker Desktop. Check: docker run hello-world. On a cluster, use Singularity or Apptainer instead. Check: singularity --version.
Java 17 or newer. Check: java -version.
Nextflow, a version from 24.10 through 25.10. Check: nextflow -v. If you have a newer Nextflow, RiboPilot runs version 25.10.6 instead. To set this yourself, add export NXF_VER=25.10.6 to your shell profile.
R 4.4.0 or newer. Check: R --version.
RiboPilot, in R:
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("NMNH-OceanDNA/RiboPilot")

You do not need to download the RiboPilot container image. This will happen automatically the first time you run the pipeline.

title: Installation
text:
Check that it works
Run the test project: see Get started.

title: Installation
text:
Optional: an NCBI API key
An NCBI API key lets RiboPilot query NCBI faster. It is free to set up. The simplest place for it is your ~/.Renviron file, next to any other keys:
NCBI_API_KEY=<your key>
Restart R after you edit the file. RiboPilot then passes the key to every run and every reference build, without writing it into the project’s .config file.
Alternatively, you can pass the key to RiboPilot::new_project() as ncbi_api_key; it is then stored in the project’s .config file and shows in the Nextflow command of the run window.
Never paste your key into a screenshot, an email, or a GitHub issue.

title: Installation
text:
Upgrading RiboPilot
Run these in R, one step at a time:
# 1. Remove the installed RiboPilot
remove.packages("RiboPilot")

# 2. Restart R
#    RStudio: Session > Restart R, or run rstudioapi::restartSession()
#    Elsewhere: quit R and start it again

# 3. Install the new version
remotes::install_github("NMNH-OceanDNA/RiboPilot")

# 4. Update existing projects as needed, once per project
RiboPilot::backwards_compatibility("~/my_project")
The changelog lists what changed.
The backwards_compatibility function brings the project’s database up to date and points the project at the container image for the RiboPilot version you installed. The next run downloads that image by itself, so there is nothing to pull by hand. Your samples, results, and settings are kept. Before it changes anything, RiboPilot saves a copy of the database (.sqlite.bak.<timestamp>) and of the project’s .config (.config.bak.<timestamp>) in the project folder. To see what would change without changing anything, add dry_run = TRUE.
What you see if you skip backwards_compatibility:

The database is out of date. The app does not open, and says “This project needs an update. Run backwards_compatibility(…) first.”
Only the container image is out of date. The app opens and says “Container version does not match RiboPilot”. Runs may still work, but with the code and tools in the older image.

Each image takes about 7.7 GB in Docker, or about 2.5 GB as a Singularity file. Once no project uses an old one image, remove it with docker image rm <image>; with Singularity, delete its file from your image cache (see Disk space, caches, and offline use).

title: Running on a cluster
text: On a computing cluster, RiboPilot sends each step of the pipeline to the cluster’s scheduler as a job, and runs the analysis tools in Singularity (or Apptainer). You still use the app to review results and export.

title: Running on a cluster
text:
Choose a profile
A profile tells RiboPilot/Nextflow how to submit jobs on your cluster. Two are built in and ready to use: executor = "NMNH_Hydra" and executor = "NOAA_SEDNA". Each has its own setup page: Smithsonian Hydra setup and NOAA SEDNA setup.
For any other Slurm, SGE, PBS, or LSF cluster, make a Nextflow profile once with RiboPilot::generate_config(), then pass its name to new_project():
RiboPilot::generate_config(
  "mylab_slurm",
  scheduler       = "slurm",
  queue           = "general",
  account         = "mylab",
  walltime        = "48h",
  container_cache = "/scratch/mylab/singularity"
)
RiboPilot::new_project(path = "/shared/mylab/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "/shared/mylab/my_samples.csv",
  data_path = "/shared/mylab/reads", 
  executor = "mylab_slurm")
container_cache is the folder where Singularity keeps the RiboPilot image, shared by every project that uses the profile. If you leave it out, RiboPilot uses NXF_SINGULARITY_CACHEDIR when that is set, and otherwise a containers folder inside your reference folder. Many clusters need a walltime: some reject a job that asks for none.
Profiles are saved in your own settings folder (on Linux, ~/.config/R/RiboPilot). To share one with your lab, save it in a shared folder with profile_dir, and pass the same profile_dir to new_project():
RiboPilot::generate_config(
  "mylab_slurm",
  scheduler   = "slurm",
  queue       = "general",
  walltime    = "48h",
  profile_dir = "/shared/mylab/ribopilot_profiles"
)
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path        = "/shared/mylab/my_project",
  mapping_fn  = "/shared/mylab/my_samples.csv",
  data_path   = "/shared/mylab/reads",
  executor    = "mylab_slurm",
  profile_dir = "/shared/mylab/ribopilot_profiles"
)

Manual profile edits. You can manually adjust profiles in the profile_dir. This may be necessary for clusters that use a customized job scheduler. If you are unsure how to do this, please consult your cluster’s job submission documentation or contact a cluster admin. For additional guidance, check NF-core to see if your cluster already has a custom config or instructions.

title: Running on a cluster
text:
Put everything on shared storage
The project folder, the reads, the reference folder, and the R library that holds RiboPilot must be visible from the login node and from every compute node.

title: Running on a cluster
text:
Open the app
On RStudio Server, just run RiboPilot::RiboPilot("/shared/mylab/my_project").
Without RStudio Server, run R and start the app on the login node or an interactive session to reach it from your own computer through an SSH tunnel:
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("/shared/mylab/my_project", port = 8123,
                     launch.browser = FALSE)
The app prints the address to open and the tunnel command. On your own computer, in a terminal:
ssh -N -L 8123:localhost:8123 you@login.cluster.edu
Then open http://localhost:8123 in your browser.
When a batch scheduler (sbatch, qsub, or bsub) is on the PATH, or the app runs on RStudio Server, the run window offers a job script to submit instead of Run from App. The headless argument of RiboPilot() overrides this:
# Always offer a job script, even when no scheduler is detected
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("/shared/mylab/my_project", headless = TRUE)

# Always offer Run from App: Nextflow runs inside the R session that
# started the app, not through the scheduler
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("/shared/mylab/my_project", headless = FALSE)
headless = FALSE only makes sense when the machine running R is allowed to do the work itself, for example an interactive compute session. Most clusters forbid heavy jobs on login nodes.

title: Running on a cluster
section: Submit a run as a job
text:
Submit a run as a job
Press Update. The run window shows the job script for the Nextflow head job. The head job is small but long-lived: 2 CPUs, 8 GB of memory, and 48 hours, in the queue and with the account from your profile. Check the partition, account, walltime, and memory, and edit the script in the window if you need to. Then press Submit as job, or Save script to submit it yourself.
The job runs on its own, so you can close the browser and watch the job with your scheduler’s tools (e.g. qstat on Hydra). Once job is done, use the reload button above the table to see new results. The app does not track a submitted job, so do not start another run for the same project until the job has finished.
Each submission leaves three kinds of files in the project’s .runs folder:

.runs/jobs/: the job scripts;
.runs/logs/: the scheduler’s log for each job;
.runs/nextflow/: one Nextflow log per run.

Once a job has finished, use Run Reports in the toolbar to see how it went.
In the Assemble step, Work Dirs finds the pipeline’s working folders for a sample, from both app runs and cluster jobs.

title: Test project: Assemble
text: Test project: 0. Get started 1. Taxonomy 2. Reference 3. Assemble 4. Annotation Review 5. Export

title: Test project: Assemble
text:
Run the pipeline
To start the pipeline, press Update. The run window says how many samples will run and shows the Nextflow command:



The run window, with the number of samples to run and the Nextflow command


Resume previous run? reuses work so that a stopped or failed run picks up where it left off. Leave it ticked.
Press Run from App. Progress shows in the window, one line per step:

HYDRA Submit as job. Press Submit as job in place of Run from App; see Submit a run as a job.




Progress of a running pipeline



Keep this browser tab open and the computer awake while running the pipeline. Closing the tab or pressing Stop stops the run; see Stopping and resuming a run.

One pipeline run does everything for each sample: it cleans the reads, assembles the rDNA, picks and scores the contigs, compares them with GenBank, maps the reads back to compute depth statistics, annotates the five features, runs the quality checks, and proposes which contigs to keep. The test run takes about 20 minutes.
When the run ends, the app reports how it went. A clean run says “Run finished with no failures.” Otherwise it shows a report that names every sample that failed. In the test project one sample fails on purpose:



End-of-run summary naming the sample that failed


If a step of the pipeline stops with an error, the report also names the sample, the step, the error code, and the likely cause. The Troubleshooting page explains how to interpret the report in more detail.
You can examine these reports later by clicking the Run Reports button in the top right corner of the app.

title: Test project: Assemble
text:
Examine the results
The Assemble table has one row per sample:



The Assemble table after the first run


The columns to look at first:

State: a green check means the sample finished; a red triangle means it failed. Hover over the icon to see what it means.
Lock: shows an open lock icon until you lock the sample.
Checks: summary of all quality checks for the sample. Red means a potentially serious issue, amber is worth a look but possibly benign, green is ok, and gray means there was nothing to compare with. See The Checks column.
# Paths, # Contigs, and # Kept: how many assembly paths and contigs the assembly produced, and how many contigs are kept. 0 kept contigs means there is nothing to export.
ITSx Warnings: shows any issues reported by the ITSx check; see the ITSx check.
Notes: what the pipeline noted about the sample, for example why it failed.
User Notes: your own notes on the sample, typed in the Notes box at the bottom of its details window.

In the Assemble step, you mostly choose which contigs to keep or drop. Trimming contigs and adjusting gene boundaries happens in the Annotation Review step.
RiboPilot runs a triage process during the pipeline that automatically keeps or drops contigs. Use the Triage button at the top of the app to modify how the triage rules work and run the process again for selected samples. Quality checks and flags explains the triage rules.

title: Test project: Assemble
text:
View sample assembly details
Click a sample’s ID to open its details. This window lists the sample’s contigs, each with K (keep) and D (drop) buttons, as well as other information like coverage, features annotated, and the verdict from the BLAST screen.
Clicking a contig row in the table highlights that row in blue. The BLAST evidence, Coverage and windowed BLAST, and Windowed BLAST details panels all show information for the highlighted contig.
When a sample has more than one assembly path, the details window also shows Compare assembly paths: the contigs that cover the same part of the rDNA repeat, aligned together. Contigs that do not overlap the others, such as a fragment covering a different part of 28S, are left out. Red ticks on the Differences track mark the columns where the paths disagree; use the arrow buttons to step through them. Zoom in to see the bases; a red column marks a difference. Each row shows its own annotated features, so you can see whether a difference falls inside a gene.
CHIM01 is an artificial chimeric contig, crated by joining sequence data from Penicillium mold and the fish species Upeneus parvus. The BLAST evidence shows that the best overall match is a Penicillium mold:



CHIM01’s BLAST evidence, with its best match a Penicillium mold


The Coverage and windowed BLAST viewer shows more detail about the chimeric sequence. In the Window BLAST taxon track, segments are colored by BLAST taxonomic match (gray is the sample’s own lineage, yellow in this case represents the mold sequence). A dashed red line marks approximate position of the join between the fish and the mold sequences, near 2,625 bp. You can hover over the track to see more details.
The Windowed BLAST details panel provides more detail about the BLAST results for each section of the chimeric contig.



CHIM01 in the sequence viewer, with the join between the fish and the mold marked

title: Test project: Assemble
text:
Rescue a sample that failed
One sample in the test project is expected to fail: every contig assembled for SRR22396893 is shorter than the default 500 bp minimum. Its State shows a red triangle. The sample’s details window shows additional information:



Details of a failed sample, with the reason and the next step


To try fixing the failed sample:

Click that sample’s Assembly Options cell.
Type a new name in Parameter set name, for example baited, and tick Edit.
Under Assembler, choose SPAdes, baited to the seed DB.
Press Save. The sample is set to Ready to run.
Press Update, then Run from App.




Assembly options set to the baited SPAdes assembler



HYDRA CPUs and memory are per-job requests. On Hydra the CPUs and Memory (GB) in an options window become each job’s request to the scheduler. A request of more than 8 GB per CPU is flagged as a high-memory job automatically. See the Hydra wiki for the compute nodes on offer.

When the run finishes, open SRR22396893’s details again. Baited SPAdes recovers four contigs over 500 bp, but none spans the whole 18S-to-28S region. Read depth for all of the contigs is low, which is likely why the we cannot assemble a larger contig.



Baited SPAdes contigs for SRR22396893: four partial pieces of 18S, ITS1, and 28S


For more information about assemblers in RiboPilot, see Choosing an assembly method

title: Test project: Assemble
text:
Lock samples when done
Select one or more samples and press Lock. Locked samples now appear in the Annotation Review step. For this test run, lock all 12 passing samples. When Lock asks about CHIM01, press Lock anyway, so you can see how the Export step will warn you about problematic contigs.

title: Disk space, caches, and offline use
text:
What needs the internet

The machine that runs Nextflow downloads the container image (from Docker Hub), and a pinned Nextflow version when yours is newer than RiboPilot supports (from GitHub).
The compute nodes reach NCBI: to download reference sequences during a run, to BLAST a contig at NCBI when the bundled rDNA database in the container finds nothing, and for the Reference step’s record counts and database builds.
The R session that runs the app downloads NCBI’s taxonomy (ftp.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov) the first time you press Assign Taxonomy.

title: Disk space, caches, and offline use
section: Running with no internet on compute nodes
text:
Running with no internet on compute nodes

Where there is internet, pull the image once: singularity pull ribopilot_<version>.sif docker://macguigand/ribopilot:<version>.
Create the project with that file as its container, for example container = "/shared/sif/ribopilot_<version>.sif" in RiboPilot::new_project().
Set NXF_VER to your Nextflow version, and run Nextflow once where there is internet, so that version is cached.
Build the reference databases beforehand, where there is internet.
Optionally, export NXF_OFFLINE=true.

An offline run still assembles and annotates every sample. Contigs the bundled rDNA database cannot match get the contaminant_unchecked warning and the triage flag “BLAST screen has not run”. The low_identity check is skipped with no warning for genes whose reference sequences are not already in your reference folder. Once you are online again, set those samples to Ready to run and press Update with Resume previous run? ticked to fill them in.

title: Get started
text:
RiboPilot takes genome-skim reads and assembles a GenBank-ready record of the nuclear ribosomal DNA repeat (rDNA). Starting a project requires only a few R commands, everything else happens in a R Shiny app.
If you use MitoPilot, this will feel familiar. RiboPilot has a similar layout, it takes the same mapping file, and it can run on the same samples. However, RiboPilot uses the Taxon column in the map file throughout the pipeline. Try to provide the species ID whenever possible, although higher level taxonomic groups should work too. See Your own project.
This guide walks through the test project, a set of 12 samples that ships with RiboPilot: 10 fish genome skims and 2 synthetic samples made to test the checks. We recommend trying the test project before you start on your own data.

title: Get started
text:
Setup
Before we begin, follow the installation instructions to get RiboPilot set up on your computer or cluster.
The test project (12 samples) took about 20 minutes on a Linux workstation with 16 CPU cores and 61 GB of memory. RiboPilot caps every task at your computer’s CPUs and memory, so a small computer runs more slowly rather than failing.

title: Get started
text:
Samples, contigs, and records
A sample is one row of your mapping file and usually corresponds to one specimen. Assembling a sample can produce more than one path (alternate ways to join the same reads), and each path can hold one or more contigs. Each contig you keep becomes one record in your GenBank export. A sample with one record is named by its ID. A sample with more than one record gets names like SRR33849683_p1_s2 (path 1, contig 2). Export files call the contig number scaffold.

title: Get started
text:
Create the test project
In R, run:
RiboPilot::new_test_project(path = "~/ribopilot_test")
This downloads small read files that hold only each sample’s rDNA reads (a few MB per sample) and sets up the project. The first run later downloads the RiboPilot container image once (about 2.6 GB).

HYDRA Project setup. Pass executor = "NMNH_Hydra", so the work goes to compute nodes and runs in Singularity instead of Docker:
RiboPilot::new_test_project(
  path = "/pool/public/genomics/<USER>/RiboPilot/test_project",
  executor = "NMNH_Hydra"
)
Put projects under /pool or /scratch. Home folders are far too small. By default Singularity’s download cache and the reference folder also sit in your home folder; Disk space, caches, and offline use shows how to move them.

While RiboPilot is in private preview, this download needs a GitHub token; see Installation. You may also see two warnings that the default fish reference database is not reachable. That is expected: RiboPilot does not ship a reference database, and the Reference step builds the ones the test project needs.
The 10 fish are real genome skims from NCBI’s Sequence Read Archive. CHIM00 and CHIM01 are synthetic: CHIM00 is a clean copy of one fish’s rDNA, and CHIM01 joins that fish’s 18S to the 28S of a Penicillium mold. CHIM01 is there so you can see the checks catch a mixed-up record.

title: Get started
text:
Open the app
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("~/ribopilot_test")
HYDRA Run the same command from RStudio Server; see Smithsonian Hydra setup.
The app opens in your browser on the Taxonomy step. The toolbar shows the five steps in order, and each step has its own table. Click a row to select it, or tick the box in the header to select every row still shown. Click a sample’s ID or its details button see additional information. Download selected rows and Download all rows under each table save it as a CSV file.



The app as it first opens, on the Taxonomy step


Two buttons appear in every step:

State sets whether a row runs the next time you press Update. The pipeline sets states itself; use the button to override one. There are five states:






State


Meaning






 On hold


Skipped by the next Update until you set it to Ready to run




 Ready to run


Queued: the next Update will process it




 In progress


Being processed by the running pipeline




 Success


Finished without errors




 Failed


Open the sample’s details to see why and what to try next





On Annotation Review, State offers only Ready to run, which queues a contig for that step’s own Update, and On hold, which keeps it out. A contig the pipeline has not finished annotating shows a sixth state there, Waiting for Assemble Update; see Test project: Annotation Review.

Lock means “I am done with this step for these rows”. Locked rows cannot have their analysis options for that step changed, the next update does not re-run them, and they move on to the next step. You can unlock at any time.

The lock and state icons at the left of each row are buttons too: clicking a row’s lock icon locks or unlocks that row alone, and clicking its state icon sets the state of that row alone.

title: Get started
text:
Test project walkthrough
The app has five steps. Each page below walks through one of them with the test project. Do them in order:

1. Taxonomy 2. Reference 3. Assemble 4. Annotation Review 5. Export

title: Get started
text:
Where to go next
After the walkthrough, Your own project shows how to write a mapping file and set up a project for your samples. If you work on a computing cluster, read Running on a cluster; if something goes wrong, see Troubleshooting.

title: Reference databases
text: To assemble a sample, RiboPilot compares its reads with known ribosomal sequences from a reference database of related organisms. A new project has no usable database until you build one in the app’s Reference step. You do not need to find or format any sequences yourself, and a database can be reused by every later project on that group.

title: Reference databases
text:
The Reference step
The Reference step comes between the Taxonomy and Assemble steps. Set up a database for every group before you assemble.
After resolving the sample taxonomy, open the Reference step and press Propose groups. RiboPilot looks at each sample’s lineage and groups samples that can share one reference database. RiboPilot picks the narrowest group containing your samples that contains at least at least 1,000 GenBank rDNA records. Samples from very different parts of the tree end up in different groups, each with its own reference database.
After defining groups, the Reference page automatically switches from a samples table to a groups table. Each row is one proposed group. The Status column says where that group stands (“Needs a database”, “Building”, “Ready”, “Build failed”, or “Left on current database”), and the rest of the row shows the clade, how many of your samples it covers, how many GenBank records matched the clade’s search (# GenBank Hits), and, once built, how many sequences the database holds (# Database Sequences). The second number is usually much smaller: the build keeps one copy of each identical sequence and drops short records. RefSeq genome annotations list many identical rDNA copies per genome, so a clade with many sequenced genomes can lose most of its hits this way. For example, Actinopteri had about 43,900 hits but built to about 12,100 sequences.

Setting a group up
The link at the right-hand end of each row says what that group needs: Set up database, Try again, or Change. Click it and you are offered four choices:

Download sequences from GenBank. The normal choice. Opens a run window, then press Run from App to download the database. When the build finishes, RiboPilot points the group’s unlocked samples at the new database. A database that already exists in your reference folder is automatically used, not rebuilt.
Use a database I already have. Points the group at a database built earlier, in this project or by someone else sharing the reference folder.
Change which clade this group uses. Lists the group’s lineage from the broadest rank to the narrowest. Pick another rank to widen or narrow the group, or search for another clade. If some samples in the group are not contained in the clade you select, they are split off into a different group. Clicking the group’s Clade cell opens the same window.
Leave these samples on their current database. Nothing is built. Use it only when you have already set a database in these samples’ Assembly Options yourself.

To handle several groups at once, tick their rows first, then click the link on any one of them. The “change clade” option is offered only for a single group.
If you press Update in the Assemble step while some groups have no database, RiboPilot warns you but goes ahead, and those samples fail.

title: Reference databases
text:
The reference folder
Built databases live in a reference folder that can be shared across projects. You can set the location of the reference folder using the Settings button (which also lets you adjust the minimum and maximum record counts the grouping step uses). Or you can set the reference folder when you create a project.
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path       = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads",
  ref_dir    = "~/ribopilot_refs"
)
If you do not set a folder, RiboPilot uses a folder in your home directory. RiboPilot::ribopilot_ref_dir() prints the folder path.
On a cluster, we recommend setting the reference folder somowhere other than your home directory where disk quotas are lower: see Disk space, caches, and offline use.

title: Choosing an assembly method
text:
RiboPilot can build the ribosomal repeat from your reads in three ways. GetOrganelle is the default. The other two use SPAdes and are there for samples GetOrganelle cannot assemble: baited assembles only the reads that match the reference database, and de-novo assembles every read.
The method is chosen per sample, under Assembler in the Assembly Options window of the Assemble step. Everything after assembly (quality checks, annotation, export) works the same whichever you pick.
If you already have an assembly for a sample, you can skip assembly altogether. See Already have an assembly?.

text:
At a glance

title: Choosing an assembly method
text:
How long each one takes
One sample from the test project, run three times on the same desktop with each assembler, gives a sense of scale. The sample (SRR14163830, a pufferfish) has 1.4 million read pairs of 2 x 150 bp. Each run had 6 CPUs and up to 24 GB of memory. The times and memory are for the assembly step alone; the rest of the workflow (read cleanup, quality checks, annotation) added about two minutes in every case.










GetOrganelle
SPAdes, baited
SPAdes, de-novo




Assembly time
1 min 20 s
19 s

2.9 GB

1 (8,960 bp)

GetOrganelle gave the whole repeat in one piece. Baited SPAdes was the fastest by far, but split the same repeat into three contigs. De-novo SPAdes took about thirty times longer than GetOrganelle, and about a hundred times longer than baited, and left more fragments to review. Larger read sets scale these numbers up, and de-novo scales up the most.

Where to start. Use GetOrganelle for the whole project. Switch a sample to baited SPAdes when it fails. Keep de-novo SPAdes for the few samples that neither of the others can assemble.

title: Choosing an assembly method
text:
GetOrganelle
GetOrganelle starts from a seed database of known ribosomal sequences, recruits the reads that match, and extends outward from them round after round. A label database then picks out which parts of the result are ribosomal. Both databases come from the Reference step, so a database built for the right group matters more here than any option.
The GetOrganelle options box carries its command-line flags. The GetOrganelle wiki explains them.

title: Choosing an assembly method
text:
SPAdes, baited
Baited assembly is the first thing to try on a sample that failed. Reads are mapped to the seed database with Bowtie 2, only the read pairs that match are kept, and SPAdes assembles that small pool. Contigs that match the label database are kept; the rest are discarded.
Because the read pool is small, this is quick and light on memory. The cost is that a read must resemble the reference to be kept. The genes (18S, 5.8S, 28S) are conserved and recruit well. The spacers between them vary much more, so on a sample distant from everything in the database a contig can end early or break at a spacer.
Two boxes control it:

bowtie2 options. How reads are matched to the seed database. The default is --local.
SPAdes options. The default is --isolate. If SPAdes rejects the reads with these flags, the run is retried once with no extra flags.

title: Choosing an assembly method
text:
SPAdes, de-novo
De-novo assembly skips the baiting step and gives SPAdes every read. The reference database is used only afterwards, to keep the contigs that match the label database. Nothing is filtered up front, so this can recover a repeat whose reads the seed database fails to recruit.
It is also by far the most expensive method, since it assembles all of the sequencing reads. Raise Memory (GB) in the Assembly Options window if a sample fails for lack of memory. Only the SPAdes options box applies.

title: Choosing an assembly method
text:
Mixing methods in one project
Since assembly options are saved as named sets, a project can use GetOrganelle for most samples and SPAdes for the difficult ones. Open a sample’s Assembly Options cell, type a new Parameter set name, tick Edit, choose the assembler, and press Save. The Assemble walkthrough shows this on a failed test sample.
A GenBank submission records one assembly method. If an export group mixes assemblers, the Export step offers to split it.

title: Test project: Export
text:
Test project: 0. Get started 1. Taxonomy 2. Reference 3. Assemble 4. Annotation Review 5. Export

Tick the contigs and press Assign Group, then type a group name. This becomes a folder name, so use only letters, digits, dot, dash, and underscore, and start with a letter, digit, or underscore.



Assigning contigs to an export group


A GenBank submission records one assembly method, so if the group mixes assemblers, RiboPilot offers to split it by assembler. In the test project the rescued sample was assembled with SPAdes, so a group named practice splits into practice-getorganelle and practice-bait.
Press Export Data, select the group, the header template, and which extra files to write:



The Export window, with the header template and the files to write


Click the Export button to generate the files.
Before it writes anything, the Export process lists every contig that the BLAST screen or the chimera check flagged, and that you have not marked Reviewed. In the test project, CHIM01 is listed. Select Leave them out.



The Export window asking about CHIM01 before it is exported


The export ends with a summary, which points out any records that may be a submission risk. Since we left out CHIM01, the summary only shows the ITSx warnings. See the the ITSx check for more details.



Export summary, with the ITSx counts


Each export group gets its own folder, out/export/<group>/. Use the Open folder button to see the results. For more details, see what is in the export folder.

HYDRA Buttons that open folders. On RStudio Server, Open folder shows the export folder in the Files pane of your RStudio session.

Exporting a group again replaces its folder, but the app warns you first.
If this was a real project, we could now proceed to GenBank submission, Take a look at Preparing a GenBank submission for more details.

HYDRA Getting files off the cluster. Export runs inside the app, not as a cluster job. To submit to GenBank, first download the export folder to your own computer.

title: Metadata field reference
text:
GBIF notes
GBIF interprets the records it publishes, so check its values before submitting:

gbif_lat_lon is empty when GBIF flags the coordinates ZERO_COORDINATE, COORDINATE_INVALID, or COORDINATE_OUT_OF_RANGE.
Other flags keep the value but are shown as badges in the viewer. Check values flagged PRESUMED_SWAPPED_COORDINATE, PRESUMED_NEGATED_LATITUDE or _LONGITUDE, COORDINATE_REPROJECTED, COORDINATE_ROUNDED, or COUNTRY_COORDINATE_MISMATCH.
Coordinates of sensitive species may be deliberately generalized. Check the dataGeneralizations and coordinateUncertaintyInMeters raw fields.
GBIF’s country is its own English name (United States of America), not always the name GenBank expects (USA). Check every source’s geo_loc_name against GenBank’s country list; marine samples use ocean or sea names from the same list.
identifiedBy and the GBIF taxon describe the museum specimen, which may differ from your identification of the sequenced tissue.

title: Test project: Reference
text:
Test project: 0. Get started 1. Taxonomy 2. Reference 3. Assemble 4. Annotation Review 5. Export

To assemble a sample, RiboPilot needs a reference database of rDNA sequences from closely related organisms. This step groups samples and builds one database from GenBank per group, which can be reused across projects.
To start, click Propose groups. RiboPilot automatically groups samples that can share a database. For the test project samples it proposes three groups. The red line warns that one of them, Actinopteri (all ray-finned fishes), holds more records than the usual maximum:



Proposed reference groups for the test samples


Click Apply to accept the proposed groups.
You should now see a Groups table. Tick all three groups and click Set up database at the end of any ticked row. The window offers Download sequences from GenBank, Use a database I already have, and Leave these samples on their current database. With only a single group ticked, it also offers Change which clade this group uses:



The choices for setting up a group’s reference database


Choose Download sequences from GenBank and press Run from App. The choice applies to every ticked group, so one run builds all three databases.

HYDRA Submit as job. Press Submit as job in place of Run from App; see Submit a run as a job. The app connects each database to the project once the job finishes.

When done, every group’s Status should read Ready:



Reference groups with their databases ready


In our test, the Syngnathiformes database (about 10,500 GenBank records) took under 3 minutes and Pleuronectiformes (about 2,300 records) under 1 minute. Actinopteri holds about 43,000 records, so its download takes much longer.
When working with your own samples, see Reference databases for more details.

title: Installing tools without a container (unsupported)
text: Not supported. RiboPilot supports Docker and Singularity only. This page keeps the old conda instructions for setups that already depend on them. They are not tested, and known gaps mean some steps fail.

title: Installing tools without a container (unsupported)
text:
The conda environment
The file environment.yml is in the RiboPilot source repository (it is not part of the installed package). With conda installed, create and activate the environment from a copy of the repository:
conda env create -f environment.yml
conda activate ribopilot
Create projects with executor = "conda"; RiboPilot warns that it is not supported:
RiboPilot::new_project(
  path       = "~/my_project",
  mapping_fn = "~/my_samples.csv",
  data_path  = "~/my_reads",
  executor   = "conda"
)
Start R from a terminal where the environment is active, so the app and Nextflow find the tools. The console functions can also put the environment on the PATH for you with conda_env:
RiboPilot::run_assembly("~/my_project", conda_env = "ribopilot")
RiboPilot::build_reference_db(
  '"Littorinimorpha"[Organism]', "littorinimorpha",
  conda_env = "ribopilot"
)

title: Installing tools without a container (unsupported)
text:
Known gaps

environment.yml does not include R or RiboPilot’s R packages. Install R 4.4 and RiboPilot yourself.
Ribotyper (part of Ribovore) is not on bioconda, so the chimera check skips its ribotyper step unless you install Ribovore 1.0.5 yourself.
The bundled rDNA database is only in the container, so every BLAST screen search goes to NCBI.

title: Installing tools without a container (unsupported)
text:
BLAST errors about GNUTLS
If a run reports a BLAST error mentioning “GNUTLS” or “secure session”, the BLAST in your environment is too old to connect to NCBI. Update it, then run the pipeline again:
conda install -n ribopilot 'blast=2.17.0'
Environments created from the current environment.yml already include a new enough version.

title: NMNH voucher submissions
text:
This page is for GenBank submissions containing specimens from the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History (NMNH). Other users can skip it.
NMNH asks that each GenBank record from one of its specimens carry the specimen voucher and the specimen’s EZID in the following format:
Not sure how to find the specimen EZIDs for your samples? Consult your department’s data manager.

title: NMNH voucher submissions
text:
Steps

Turn it on. In Export Data, tick NMNH user. RiboPilot adds [specimen_voucher={nmnh_specimen_voucher}] [voucherURI={nmnh_voucherURI}] to the FASTA header templates, including the per-marker template. If the template already has either modifier, it asks before replacing it. The switch is remembered when the header template is saved.
Check the status. The NMNH user box shows how many samples need attention, or “All N samples ready”.
Review and fix samples in the voucher report.
Export as usual. Exporting with problems asks first, and an empty [specimen_voucher=] or [voucherURI=] is left out of the header.




NMNH user ticked: where each value comes from and how many samples need attention

title: NMNH voucher submissions
text:
Where the values come from
For each sample, RiboPilot takes the first valid value from, in order:

your mapping file (pick the Catalog number column and Specimen link column under Optional: take these from mapping file columns),
the linked GBIF record,
the NCBI BioSample,
the GEOME record.

A voucher with no EZID is looked up in GBIF to find the EZID, and an EZID with no voucher is looked up to find the voucher. Linking the samples first (see Linking records across databases) fills in more values.

title: NMNH voucher submissions
text:
What is checked and fixed

Voucher: must be USNM:<collection>:<catalog> with an NCBI collection code (FISH, Birds, MAMM, Herp, IZ, ENT, Botany), or US:<catalog> for botany. Letter case and repeated USNM prefixes are fixed. USNM:LAB tissue numbers are rejected.
EZID: written as http://n2t.net/ark:/65665/3... and checked against GBIF. A tissue EZID is replaced with its parent specimen’s, and the voucher must match the GBIF record. A media EZID is rejected. GBIF’s answers are cached in the project; Re-check with GBIF asks again.

title: NMNH voucher submissions
text:
The voucher report
Review and fix (or Review NMNH values) opens the report. It has two tables: Need attention or marked Not NMNH, and Pass the NMNH check. Each cell shows the value, where it came from, and the result; click its ? for details. The Auto-fixed column marks samples whose values RiboPilot corrected.
To fix a sample:

Type a value into the cell. It is checked when you leave the cell and saved in the project; your mapping file is not changed. Clear the cell to go back to the automatic value.
Pick a field under the cell to take the value from another mapping-file column or metadata field, or None to leave the modifier out.
Tick Not NMNH for samples that are not NMNH specimens. Their values are used as found, without NMNH checks.
Click the sample ID to open its metadata; Back to voucher report returns.
To easily edit many samples, use Download CSV for bulk edit, edit the file, then Upload edited CSV.




NMNH voucher report with a rejected tissue number, a Not NMNH sample, and a voucher that does not match GBIF

title: NOAA SEDNA setup
text:
This page covers what is specific to the NOAA NMFS SEDNA cluster. Once you are set up here, RiboPilot works as in the Get started walkthrough, with executor = "NOAA_SEDNA". Running on a cluster explains how RiboPilot uses a cluster in general.
You need a SEDNA account; see the account instructions, or contact Krista Nichols (krista.nichols@noaa.gov).

title: NOAA SEDNA setup
text:
First-time setup
RiboPilot needs Nextflow, Singularity, and R. On SEDNA, put all three in one Mamba environment; installing RiboPilot with the cluster’s R module runs into problems.
Log in to the NOAA NMFS VPN, then to SEDNA. If you have never used Mamba on SEDNA, run this once:
/opt/bioinformatics/mambaforge/bin/mamba init
Create the environment. This may take a while.
mamba create --name RiboPilot_deps 'bioconda::nextflow>=24.10,<25.11' \
  conda-forge::singularity conda-forge::zlib 'conda-forge::r-base>=4.4' -y
Then install RiboPilot into it:
mamba activate RiboPilot_deps
R
In that R session, follow step 5 of Install the tools, then leave R with quit().
To upgrade later, activate RiboPilot_deps first, then follow Upgrading RiboPilot.

title: NOAA SEDNA setup
text:
Open the app
The app needs little computing power, since the heavy work goes to the queue. Start a small interactive session, note the name of the node it gives you, and start R:
srun -c 2 --mem=16GB -p standard --pty /bin/bash
hostname
mamba activate RiboPilot_deps
R
In R, create a project (once), then open the app without a browser:
RiboPilot::new_test_project(
  path = "/path/to/RiboPilot/test_project",
  executor = "NOAA_SEDNA"
)
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("/path/to/RiboPilot/test_project",
  host = "0.0.0.0", port = 8123, launch.browser = FALSE)
Use the same executor = "NOAA_SEDNA" with RiboPilot::new_project() for your own data. Keep projects on shared project or scratch space, not in your home folder. Disk space, caches, and offline use shows how to move Singularity’s caches and the reference folder there too.
On your own computer, open a tunnel to that node, using the name hostname printed:
ssh -N -L 8123:<node>:8123 <user>@sedna.nwfsc2.noaa.gov
Enter your password; if it works, nothing more is printed. Then open http://localhost:8123 in Chrome or Firefox. Leave both terminals open while you use the app.

The app has no login. Other SEDNA users can reach its port. Pick an unusual port number, and close the app when you are done.

title: NOAA SEDNA setup
text:
Run the pipeline
Press Update. The run window shows a Slurm job script for the standard partition. Press Submit as job, or Save script to submit it yourself with sbatch. The job keeps going after you close the browser and the interactive session. Watch it with squeue, then press the reload button above the table to see new results. Submit a run as a job has the details.
The job needs Nextflow and Singularity. A job submitted from the app inherits the RiboPilot_deps environment. If you submit a saved script from a new terminal, run mamba activate RiboPilot_deps there first.

title: RiboPilot
text:
RiboPilot 

 
Please see the documentation website for more details.
RiboPilot is a product of the NMNH Ocean DNA initiative and does not represent an official Smithsonian Institution position or product.
RiboPilot assembles and annotates the nuclear ribosomal DNA repeat (rDNA) from genome skimming data, then helps you check and clean up the result and package it for submission to GenBank. If you already have an assembly, RiboPilot can start from that instead of reads. RiboPilot is a companion to MitoPilot, which does the same process for the mitochondrial genome. You can run both tools on the same samples and get both marker sets from one sequencing run.
Most of your work happens in a point-and-click Shiny app that runs in your web browser. The step-by-step Get started guide walks through a complete project from start to finish.


The nuclear ribosomal DNA unit
Every cell carries the ribosomal RNA genes in a repeated unit that is copied hundreds to thousands of times in a row. Because there are so many copies, even a shallow, inexpensive “genome skim” sequences this region very deeply. From it you get some widely used nuclear markers for phylogenetics and DNA barcoding: 18S, 28S, ITS1, ITS2, and the full ITS region.

The core rDNA unit is typically highly conserved, but with hundreds of copies arranged in a tandem repeat. The three ribosomal genes (18S, 5.8S, 28S) are highly conserved and act as anchors. The two spacers (ITS1, ITS2) sit between them, evolve quickly, and are the regions that distinguish closely related species.
Between the 28S of one copy and the 18S of the next lies the intergenic spacer (IGS): the 3’ external transcribed spacer (ETS), a non-transcribed spacer (NTS), and the 5’ ETS of the next copy (Hwang and Kim 1999).
However, the structure of the nuclear rDNA repeat varies across the tree of life. The IGS can range from a few hundred base pairs to tens of kilobases and often holds subrepeats. Repeat blocks of the rDNA unit can be located at one or several places in the genome. See Wang et al. 2023 for a review.


What RiboPilot does for you
The app walks each project through five steps, in order:

Taxonomy. RiboPilot matches the Taxon you provide for each sample to the NCBI taxonomy. Samples must be reviewed and locked here before they move on to assembly, since the taxonomic ID of your samples guides scoring and curation.
Reference. RiboPilot groups related samples and builds a reference database of known rDNA sequences for each group, from GenBank.
Assemble. One run cleans the reads, assembles the ribosomal repeat for each sample, picks the best assembly path, finds the five features (18S, ITS1, 5.8S, ITS2, 28S), and checks each result for problems such as a missing gene, an unusual length, a possible contaminant, or a chimera. You choose which contigs to keep or drop for the next step.
Annotation Review. You check the annotated features and quality flags of each kept contig, adjusting boundaries if needed.
Export. RiboPilot writes a tidy, GenBank-ready submission package, and warns you about any flagged record first.

Behind the scenes RiboPilot uses established bioinformatics tools (fastp, GetOrganelle, barrnap / pybarrnap, ITSx, BLAST, and others) and stitches them together for you. You do not need to learn or run any of them yourself. However, advanced users can adjust the parameters for each tool within RiboPilot.


Taxonomic Scope
Each group of samples needs a reference database of known rDNA sequences. You build it once per group in the app, from GenBank. See the reference database guide.
RiboPilot also runs automatic quality checks tuned for a taxonomic group. Five settings ship, picked from each sample’s lineage: a generic animal setting, and settings for ray-finned fishes, sea stars, true jellyfish, and octocorals; see the curation guide. These settings are still in development and likely need fine tuning.


Installation
RiboPilot requires Docker (or Singularity on a cluster), Java, Nextflow, and R. The Installation guide lists versions and checks. Then, in R:
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("NMNH-OceanDNA/RiboPilot")


Getting started
The best way to learn RiboPilot is to run the built-in test project. The first command downloads the test samples and sets everything up; the second opens the app:
RiboPilot::new_test_project(path = "~/ribopilot_test")
RiboPilot::RiboPilot("~/ribopilot_test")
By default this fetches small rDNA-filtered read subsets published with the RiboPilot releases, so setup takes under a minute. Pass full_size = TRUE to download the complete read sets from ENA/SRA instead (several GB). The first run also downloads the container image once (about 2.6 GB).
Follow the Get started guide to walk through project initialization and the five steps in the app.


Citing RiboPilot
Run citation("RiboPilot") in R.


Getting help

Full documentation: https://nmnh-oceandna.github.io/RiboPilot/
When something goes wrong: the Troubleshooting guide.
Questions or problems: please open an issue.

title: Annotate every record in a multi-record fasta

Details
barrnap reports coordinates in the input frame; on a genuinely minus-strand
record those anchors run 28S -> 5.8S -> 18S in ascending position, the
opposite of the ascending order reconcile_features()'s spacer-clipping

its regions in the frame where the anchors DO ascend. So minus-strand
records are reconciled in that revcomp frame – barrnap's anchors are
flipped into it, ITSx's output is used as reported – and the finished
model is flipped back to the input frame afterward.
